questions.title: Place the language boundary
questions.stem: A seed laboratory receives narrative field observations and numerical germination counts. Scientists already use a validated formula to calculate the certified germination percentage. They want faster preparation of explanatory notes, but the certificate calculation must remain reproducible. A pilot can identify relevant observations with source links. The release budget permits one integration this quarter. Which initial architecture BEST fits the evidence?

options.text: Draft source-linked observation notes beside the existing formula result, leaving certification calculations in the validated laboratory service.
options.why: This uses demonstrated language capability without changing the reproducible calculation that already satisfies the laboratory requirement.

options.text: Have Claude compute percentages and explanations together, then compare only the prose against the scientists’ existing notes.
options.why: The comparison would leave the changed numerical calculation unvalidated, despite reproducibility being an explicit release constraint here.

options.text: Build an autonomous research agent that chooses formulas from the observation text and submits completed laboratory certificates.
options.why: Formula selection and certificate submission introduce new authority beyond the demonstrated benefit and the stated integration scope.

options.text: Use the existing numerical formula to generate every explanation through templates before evaluating the narrative extraction pilot.
options.why: Templates may help, but this discards demonstrated language value without testing whether fixed text covers the field observations.

questions.decision: Use the demonstrated language capability where it helps scientists interpret observations, while preserving the validated numerical calculation. The useful boundary lies between preparing an explanation and computing a certified quantity; combining both under model control adds risk without addressing an unmet need.

questions.title: A measurable launch envelope
questions.stem: A festival accessibility team wants a multilingual information assistant before ticket sales open. The sponsor asks the architect to choose a model now, although no one has agreed what acceptable service means. Staff can review sample answers, and venue policies are available. Which TWO findings should be established as requirements before choosing the model and orchestration pattern?

options.text: Require exactly three specialist agents because the event supports three languages and each language deserves isolated reasoning.
options.why: The number of languages alone does not establish an orchestration need or measurable quality, latency, and capacity expectations.

options.text: Agree how quickly venue changes must appear in answers and who supplies authoritative updates during the event.
options.why: Freshness and source ownership constrain the data path and operational responsibilities rather than presupposing a particular technical design.

options.text: Agree supported languages, peak concurrent demand, and the maximum user-visible response time at the ticket-sale launch.
options.why: These define observable service expectations that affect model selection, load planning, and evaluation before implementation choices are locked.

options.text: Use the sponsor’s favorite demonstration as the launch baseline without measuring staff work or expected attendee demand.
options.why: A demonstration provides examples but cannot establish the current baseline or the volume and constraints of the real service.

options.text: Choose a vector database first and treat its default retrieval settings as the assistant’s acceptance criteria.
options.why: A component default describes implementation behavior; it does not establish the service outcome festival users and operators require.

questions.decision: Requirements must constrain an architectural choice in observable terms. Language coverage and a demand envelope drive quality and capacity testing; an accepted freshness rule constrains integration. Preferred components and impressive demonstrations cannot substitute for a service definition the owners will evaluate.

questions.title: Repair only the presentation
questions.stem: A museum kiosk explains objects using retrieved catalogue records. A public-display contract permits only text and a validated catalogue identifier; HTML and external links cannot reach the screen. Curators confirm that the factual drafts are accurate, but some outputs contain Markdown links. The team wants to keep useful drafts while enforcing the display contract before delivery. Which design BEST establishes that boundary?

options.text: Parse a constrained response, validate catalogue identifiers, and render escaped text through the kiosk’s existing display component.
options.why: The delivery boundary can enforce the actual interface contract independently of whether the model follows the formatting instruction.

options.text: Put the display contract in the system prompt and render the returned Markdown through a general-purpose browser component.
options.why: This still accepts unvalidated presentation syntax and changes the renderer rather than enforcing the kiosk’s permitted output contract.

options.text: Reject every visitor question containing a URL, then allow the model response through because unsafe syntax was removed upstream.
options.why: Input filtering does not constrain syntax newly generated in an answer, so it leaves the identified output failure unresolved.

options.text: Log presentation violations for curator review after displaying the answer, and tune examples during the next monthly release.
options.why: The feedback loop can improve generation but cannot prevent contract violations in answers already delivered to the public kiosk.

questions.decision: The presentation contract belongs in a deterministic boundary before rendering. Structured parsing and allowlisted identifiers can reject invalid payloads and permit bounded repair without discarding the factual generation step. A prompt helps formation but is not the enforcement mechanism for the display interface.

questions.title: Fresh facts with a failure state
questions.stem: A ferry operator’s assistant explains boarding options from the live sailing service. When that service fails, an old cache is available but its age varies. The operator requires that current departure claims use data under two minutes old; older information may be shown only as historical. Which TWO architectural behaviors preserve this contract during intermittent source failures?

options.text: Allow the model to promote cached times to current times whenever previous schedules have usually remained unchanged.
options.why: Historical stability does not establish current source freshness and therefore cannot satisfy the explicitly stated departure-information contract.

options.text: Strip cache timestamps before context assembly so the assistant uses the most relevant departure regardless of retrieval age.
options.why: Removing timestamps eliminates the evidence needed to distinguish permitted historical information from a prohibited current departure claim.

options.text: Return a clear unavailable state with the permitted historical view and the operator’s live-information contact route.
options.why: This preserves useful degraded service while distinguishing historical evidence from a current departure claim the system cannot support.

options.text: Retry the live service without a deadline while keeping the visitor’s request open until a fresh answer appears.
options.why: Unbounded waiting does not provide a controlled failure state and can consume service capacity during a prolonged source outage.

options.text: Attach retrieval time and source status to sailing results, and validate freshness before stating a current departure.
options.why: The architecture needs observable evidence age to enforce the operator’s two-minute requirement rather than infer freshness from fluent wording.

questions.decision: Freshness must travel with the evidence, and delivery must enforce its meaning. A stale result can retain historical value without supporting a current departure claim. An explicit source failure lets the application provide a useful alternative rather than silently manufacturing freshness or concealing degraded operation.

questions.title: Discover tasks before assigning them
questions.stem: An archaeology archive is migrating inconsistent collection descriptions into a new taxonomy. Some collections need only terminology changes; others reveal missing relationships that require additional investigation. A fixed initial survey can identify which collections need which follow-up work, but the follow-ups cannot all be enumerated beforehand. Each worker can operate on an isolated collection snapshot. Which pattern BEST fits this variable decomposition?

options.text: Route every collection to one of two predefined rewrite prompts and prohibit additional investigation when a relationship is missing.
options.why: The predefined routes cannot cover the newly discovered investigations that the scenario explicitly requires for some collection records.

options.text: Use an orchestrator to inspect the survey, assign bounded collection investigations, and reconcile their outputs against the new taxonomy.
options.why: Dynamic task discovery matches the variable follow-ups, while bounded worker assignments and synthesis preserve an understandable migration process.

options.text: Create one fixed parallel worker per taxonomy term and let each independently rewrite every collection that mentions its term.
options.why: Term-based fanout duplicates edits across collections and does not match the collection-specific work discovered by the initial survey.

options.text: Use a critic loop on the complete archive until the critic declares that every description has become internally consistent.
options.why: An archive-wide critic does not define bounded discovered tasks and lacks a clear method to resolve collection-level dependencies.

questions.decision: An orchestrator can discover the required work from the survey and assign bounded collection tasks, then integrate results. This is distinct from fixed sectioning because the actual subtasks emerge from the input. Isolation, result contracts, and a final consistency check remain necessary even when discovery is dynamic.

questions.title: A critic needs a measurable purpose
questions.stem: A public radio team generates brief programme descriptions. It has a precise prohibited-claims list and a rubric for whether the description faithfully reflects a recording. Independent editors can explain which failures a revision fixes. The team is considering a bounded evaluator loop instead of five independent drafts. Which TWO pieces of evidence most strongly support choosing the evaluator loop?

options.text: The evaluator writes longer explanations than human editors, demonstrating that it has inspected more evidence than the generator.
options.why: Explanation length is not evidence of accurate judgment or useful feedback and can hide verbosity bias in evaluation.

options.text: The new loop uses the same prompt and context as the generator, ensuring that no independent interpretation can disagree.
options.why: Sharing assumptions can reinforce the initial error; agreement alone does not validate the critic’s judgment or the revised description.

options.text: Five drafts frequently repeat the same mistake, so any critic model must necessarily produce a correct alternative description.
options.why: Correlated generation errors do not establish critic competence; the critic itself needs measurement against the known failure cases.

options.text: Editors can calibrate the evaluator on faithful and misleading descriptions using the same explicit claims and fidelity rubric.
options.why: A calibrated, actionable evaluation signal gives the revision process a defensible target and makes failures of the critic observable.

options.text: On held-out recordings, rubric-specific feedback produces better revised descriptions than the initial drafts within the allowed response time.
options.why: This demonstrates useful refinement under the product constraint rather than assuming that additional model calls necessarily improve the result.

questions.decision: The evaluator-optimizer pattern is supported by actionable criteria and demonstrated improvement through feedback. It is not justified simply because another model can comment. Compare the bounded loop with simpler alternatives under the same rubric, and include the extra cost and elapsed time in the decision.

questions.title: A partial worker result is evidence
questions.stem: A geological survey assistant delegates seismic, water-table, and land-use investigations. Its report must identify which observations support each recommendation. The water-table worker returns usable measurements for two of four zones and times out on the others. Retrying is allowed once within the report deadline. Which orchestration design BEST uses the successful work without implying coverage the system does not have?

options.text: Treat any nonempty worker output as success, allowing the orchestrator to infer unreported zones from neighboring measurements.
options.why: Nonempty output does not demonstrate complete coverage, and inference would conceal the missing evidence required for zone-specific recommendations.

options.text: Discard all workers’ findings and rerun the entire survey whenever any worker returns fewer measurements than originally requested.
options.why: Whole-job retries waste successful evidence and still lack a result contract that distinguishes missing coverage from completed observations.

options.text: Return covered zones, sources, and partial status; retry missing zones within budget and mark unresolved coverage in the report.
options.why: The contract preserves successful evidence and makes missing coverage visible while respecting the deadline and the allowed retry budget.

options.text: Have the seismic worker rewrite the water-table section using its own contextual knowledge so the final report remains complete.
options.why: A different worker’s contextual knowledge does not replace the missing measurements or preserve their provenance in a zone-specific report.

questions.decision: Worker results should carry scope and explicit completion status. The orchestrator can reuse successful zones, bound the retry, and preserve unresolved gaps in the final analysis. It should not collapse a partial investigation into either invented completeness or the loss of all otherwise useful evidence.

video_evidence.concept: A partial worker result is evidence

questions.title: Keep a shared budget enforceable
questions.stem: A film restoration service uses specialists to investigate damaged frames, soundtrack defects, and historical references. Costs vary widely across reels. An orchestrator currently starts more workers when any worker suggests another lead. A reel has a strict processing budget, and unfinished investigation is acceptable if disclosed. Which THREE controls together support flexible investigation while reliably bounding the service’s exposure?

options.text: Have the orchestrator rank new leads by expected value and stop expansion when the remaining reserved budget cannot fund them.
options.why: Prioritization preserves flexibility within the enforceable limit instead of allowing recursively proposed work to expand the job without bounds.

options.text: Raise the model’s maximum output length for every specialist so fewer messages appear in the job’s final activity report.
options.why: Message count is not a reliable spending boundary and longer outputs can increase cost without controlling worker or tool fanout.

options.text: Reserve worker and tool-call allowances against one job-level budget before dispatch, including concurrent work already in flight.
options.why: Atomic shared accounting prevents simultaneously launched workers from each spending what appears to be the same remaining budget.

options.text: Give workers explicit termination conditions and require structured findings with unresolved leads when their assigned allowance is exhausted.
options.why: Local bounds prevent an individual investigation from continuing indefinitely and preserve useful evidence when its allotted effort is insufficient.

options.text: Calculate total cost only after every specialist finishes, then remove low-value sections until the published report fits the budget.
options.why: Editing the report cannot recover resources already consumed, so retrospective accounting does not enforce the processing budget during investigation.

questions.decision: Flexible delegation requires enforceable resource accounting and explicit partial outcomes. Reserve a shared budget before work starts, bound workers locally, and stop expansion when the job cannot fund it. A useful result can document unresolved leads; hiding or postponing accounting cannot make an open-ended investigation bounded.

questions.title: Shared definitions before sectioning
questions.stem: A maritime heritage project extracts events from independently digitized ship logs. Workers can read different voyages in parallel, but all must distinguish a ship’s name from its registration identity and normalize dates under the same rules. Early runs contain duplicate events and conflicting identities. Which decomposition change BEST addresses the shared dependency while retaining useful parallel work across the voyages?

options.text: Establish shared identity and date rules, extract voyages independently, then reconcile overlapping events through stable source identifiers.
options.why: The shared contract and integration stage address cross-voyage consistency while preserving parallelism where the underlying reading work is independent.

options.text: Require the final writer to remove uncertain ship names without retaining the evidence that different workers used for identification.
options.why: Removing names obscures the inconsistency rather than resolving it, and discarding provenance weakens any later attempt at reconciliation.

options.text: Run every voyage extraction twice and keep the version with more events, using output volume as the consistency criterion.
options.why: More extracted events do not demonstrate accurate identity handling and can reward duplicates rather than resolving shared normalization requirements.

options.text: Assign one worker per calendar month and let each invent local ship identifiers before concatenating the resulting event lists.
options.why: Local identifiers and concatenation preserve the source of inconsistency, and month boundaries may divide events that need reconciliation.

questions.decision: Parallel workers need the common identity and normalization contract before independent extraction. A reconciliation stage then resolves overlaps using stable evidence identifiers. This targets the dependency between tasks while retaining the throughput advantage of independent reading; repeating uncoordinated passes would leave the same integration problem intact.

questions.title: Value beyond token savings
questions.stem: A textile design studio compares two assistants using the same approved quality rubric. Both meet the delivery deadline and pass the required quality threshold. The exhibit shows monthly operating cost and designer time saved; a saved hour is valued at $40 of usable design capacity, not assumed payroll reduction. Which option has the higher monthly net capacity value under this stipulated valuation?

options.text: Treat both as equivalent because meeting the quality threshold removes the need to compare their different capacity outcomes.
options.why: A common quality gate permits comparison but does not erase the measured difference in capacity value and operating cost.

options.text: Choose B: it saves $7,200 in payroll every month, regardless of staffing plans or how the studio uses freed time.
options.why: The exhibit values usable capacity; it does not establish a reduction in wages, staffing, or any other cash expenditure.

options.text: Choose A: its operating cost is $1,300 lower, so it necessarily produces more business value under the agreed valuation.
options.why: Lower expenditure alone ignores the value of the additional sixty usable designer hours supplied by the second measured option.

options.text: Choose B: its valued capacity minus operating cost is $5,000 monthly, exceeding A’s net value by $1,100.
options.why: The calculation applies the explicitly stipulated hour valuation and includes the additional operating cost rather than comparing token spend alone.

questions.decision: Option B yields 180 × $40 − $2,200 = $5,000 in net monthly capacity value. Option A yields 120 × $40 − $900 = $3,900. The additional operating cost buys enough usable design capacity to improve the stipulated net value by $1,100; this is not automatically a cash saving.

questions.title: Degraded service has a contract
questions.stem: A library research service wants resilience when its preferred model is unavailable. A candidate fallback meets citation-format checks but performs worse on complex cross-document contradictions. Librarians permit fallback for catalogue summaries, while disputed historical claims must wait for the primary route or a librarian. Which TWO design decisions make the availability improvement consistent with the accepted quality trade-off?

options.text: Keep fallback use invisible to operators and users because a successful API response demonstrates that the availability objective was met.
options.why: API success can conceal unacceptable task outcomes and prevents operators from observing the degraded behavior whose risk was explicitly accepted.

options.text: Expand the fallback’s context automatically until it matches the primary model’s quality, without rerunning the research acceptance evaluations.
options.why: More context is an untested hypothesis, not evidence that the fallback now satisfies the complex-task quality requirement.

options.text: Classify permitted fallback task classes and evaluate the fallback against their own acceptance criteria before enabling automatic substitution.
options.why: The fallback is justified for the measured catalogue-summary class, not for complex contradiction tasks whose quality bar it misses.

options.text: Measure and disclose degraded outcomes, preserving a wait or librarian route for disputed claims outside the fallback’s validated scope.
options.why: This makes the accepted quality limitation operationally visible and keeps unsupported complex claims from being counted as successful service.

options.text: Use the fallback for every request because matching citation format establishes equivalent research quality across all task classes.
options.why: Citation syntax does not measure contradiction reasoning, so a format pass cannot justify expanding fallback beyond the validated task class.

questions.decision: Fallback eligibility is a task-level contract rather than a blanket model substitution. Route only validated classes to the fallback, and expose degraded handling where the quality-sensitive class cannot be served. Availability measurements should count permitted outcomes rather than treating every HTTP success as an acceptable research answer.

questions.title: Choose from a feasible frontier
questions.stem: A botanical image-caption service has three evaluated model configurations. The owner requires at least 94% factual acceptance and a p95 completion time of at most 1.8 seconds. All measurements use the same held-out photographs and production-shaped load. Monthly costs include the full input and output workload. Which configuration should the architect recommend from the exhibit, assuming no other requirements distinguish them?

options.text: Choose P because its substantially lower monthly cost and faster responses compensate for a small factual-acceptance shortfall.
options.why: The owner defined factual acceptance as a gate, so lower cost cannot compensate for failing that independent release requirement.

options.text: Distribute traffic evenly across all three configurations so their average quality and latency represent a balanced model portfolio.
options.why: A random portfolio sends requests to configurations that independently miss requirements and lacks evidence that the combined service satisfies them.

options.text: Choose Q because the highest factual score establishes the best architecture even when its measured completion latency exceeds the limit.
options.why: The additional factual performance does not satisfy the separate latency gate, which remains binding in the stated service contract.

options.text: Choose R because it satisfies both required gates; preserve the measured workload and rerun the gates before future changes.
options.why: The selected configuration is feasible under the stated quality and latency constraints, unlike both cheaper and more accurate alternatives.

questions.decision: Configuration R alone meets both gates: 94.6% acceptance is above 94%, and 1.7 seconds is below 1.8 seconds. P is faster but fails quality; Q improves quality but misses latency. Price optimization applies within the feasible set, rather than compensating for a missed independent requirement.

questions.title: Separate policy from quotations
questions.stem: A documentary archive assistant receives curator instructions, quoted interviews, and a visitor’s question in one prompt. Some interviewees describe what an assistant should say, and those quotations sometimes influence the assistant’s style. The archive wants to preserve the quotations because they are essential evidence. Which TWO changes best improve the prompt’s interpretation without treating delimiters as a complete security boundary?

options.text: Summarize every interview into a single unattributed sentence before answering so no directive can remain visible to the model.
options.why: This discards essential evidence and provenance without establishing that the summarizer itself will handle quoted directives appropriately.

options.text: Declare the interview section fully trusted after adding XML tags and allow its text to override the curator’s system policy.
options.why: Tags clarify structure but do not change the authority of third-party evidence or justify promoting quotations above the curator’s instructions.

options.text: Remove all quotation marks from the interviews so the assistant reads every statement as one coherent instruction stream.
options.why: Removing boundaries further blurs evidence and instruction roles, increasing the exact ambiguity that the archive is trying to correct.

options.text: Explain that interview statements are evidence to analyze, and illustrate how to quote a directive without following its instruction.
options.why: A targeted example teaches the intended interpretation of the observed ambiguous content rather than merely repeating a broad behavior prohibition.

options.text: Place curator rules, reference interviews, and the live visitor question in consistently named sections with document identifiers.
options.why: Explicit structure reduces confusion between instructions and quoted evidence while retaining the provenance needed to answer the visitor’s question.

questions.decision: Clearly mark authoritative instructions, examples, and reference material, and tell the model how quotations should be used. This improves interpretation while preserving the evidence. Delimiters do not authorize actions or guarantee injection resistance; tool permissions and output controls must still enforce any actual capability boundary.

questions.title: Teach the actual audience
questions.stem: A bridge conservation assistant produces notes for trained structural inspectors. The output must distinguish observed damage, uncertain interpretation, and next inspection evidence. Current notes either explain elementary terminology or assert a diagnosis without naming missing evidence. The same source material will continue to be used. Which prompt change BEST addresses both problems while leaving technical decision authority with the inspectors?

options.text: Ask the model to sound like a senior engineer and retain the existing unstructured examples for stylistic consistency.
options.why: A tone instruction does not repair examples that fail to distinguish observed damage from interpretation or needed evidence.

options.text: Request a longer reasoning narrative for each defect so basic definitions and final diagnoses can both remain in the output.
options.why: A longer narrative preserves the audience mismatch and does not require the explicit evidential separation that the inspectors need.

options.text: Specify the inspector audience and show concise examples separating observed facts, qualified interpretations, and the evidence needed to resolve uncertainty.
options.why: The prompt directly defines both expertise level and the evidence structure missing from the current conservation notes.

options.text: Ban definitions and uncertainty words entirely, leaving inspectors only a short diagnosis that they can accept or reject.
options.why: Removing uncertainty language encourages unsupported certainty and does not provide the missing distinction between observation and technical interpretation.

questions.decision: Define the audience and the output’s evidential purpose, then demonstrate the desired separation of observation, interpretation, and unknowns. This provides the missing communication contract. Technical uncertainty should remain explicit; neither deleting all explanations nor asking for stronger confidence would make the notes useful to trained inspectors.

questions.title: Examples that expose boundaries
questions.stem: A wildlife audio classifier assigns one of five labels and a short evidence span. Its examples contain clear single-species recordings, while evaluation failures involve overlapping calls and uncertain silence. The schema already validates. The team has budget for one prompt revision before rerunning a held-out set. Which TWO changes most directly target the demonstrated generalization gap?

options.text: Add expert-checked examples showing overlapping calls, uncertain silence, and the intended label or abstention behavior for each boundary.
options.why: These examples target the missing semantic distinctions observed in evaluation rather than strengthening an already well-represented easy recording type.

options.text: Add ten more clear single-species examples because a larger example count necessarily improves classification of ambiguous overlapping calls.
options.why: Increasing coverage of the existing easy pattern does not supply the missing decision boundaries that caused the measured failures.

options.text: Mark each example and its evidence separately from the live recording metadata, then test on different held-out boundary cases.
options.why: Clear example boundaries reduce input confusion, while independent evaluation checks whether the revision generalizes beyond the examples supplied in context.

options.text: Replace all examples with a stronger schema declaration because valid labels prove the model understood the recording content.
options.why: A schema restricts response shape and label vocabulary; it does not establish that a semantically correct label was selected.

options.text: Copy the failed held-out recordings and their labels into the prompt, then report performance on those same recordings.
options.why: The reported score would measure exposure to the answers rather than generalization to previously unseen recordings at the difficult boundary.

questions.decision: The examples should represent the decision boundaries that failed, including mixed and ambiguous recordings, and should separate illustrative content from live input. Keep the evaluation set independent so the team measures generalization rather than memorization. Schema validity is useful but does not establish that the selected labels are correct.

questions.title: Budget the complete request
questions.stem: A bilingual cartography assistant accepts a base64-embedded map image, text annotations, a system policy, and several tool definitions. Character-count estimates have understated request sizes, and occasional large requests exceed the service’s configured input budget. The team must estimate before admission while retaining a margin for changes in input processing. Which design BEST replaces the unreliable estimate without confusing input and output limits?

options.text: Use the model-specific token-counting request with the actual image, annotations, policy, and tools, then apply a conservative admission margin.
options.why: The estimate reflects the full intended request rather than a text-only proxy and explicitly preserves room for estimation differences.

options.text: Count only annotation characters and divide by four because the other request components are stable across most customer sessions.
options.why: Stable content still consumes input capacity, and character ratios cannot reliably estimate images or different language tokenization patterns.

options.text: Reuse the previous request’s cached-token count as the complete estimate whenever the same user opens another map image.
options.why: Cached-token usage describes a previous prefix and cannot establish the total token count of a new multimodal request.

options.text: Lower the output-token maximum until every request is accepted, treating that cap as the exact input budget available.
options.why: The output cap does not reduce the size of the submitted image, policy, tools, or annotations already occupying input capacity.

questions.decision: Count the actual model-specific request, including its multimodal and tool content, before admission. Treat the result as an estimate and enforce a conservative service budget. Output allowance and context capacity are related constraints, but lowering the completion cap does not erase tokens already present in the input request.

questions.title: Concise output without amputation
questions.stem: A mineral identification assistant must return a complete explanation in about 120 words. Engineers reduced the output cap after several verbose responses, and valid explanations now stop before the uncertainty statement. The owner considers that statement essential. Which change BEST makes replies concise while preserving completeness, assuming the model’s supported limits are sufficient for the intended answer?

options.text: Reduce the cap further so the model learns that longer explanations are penalized and will eventually fit the essential content.
options.why: A generation cutoff is not feedback training and can make incomplete answers more frequent without teaching a better concise structure.

options.text: Keep the low cap and append the standard uncertainty sentence to every truncated response regardless of what the response already contains.
options.why: Appending a sentence cannot restore other missing content and may attach a misleading uncertainty statement to an incomplete or malformed explanation.

options.text: Specify a complete short structure with concise examples, leave headroom in the output cap, and handle truncation before showing an answer.
options.why: This steers intended length while preserving required content and distinguishes an incomplete completion from a successfully concise mineral explanation.

options.text: Remove the uncertainty requirement because an answer that fits the configured output cap is operationally easier to deliver.
options.why: This sacrifices an explicitly essential owner requirement to accommodate a configuration choice rather than resolving the underlying verbosity problem.

questions.decision: Concision should be expressed as an output contract and taught with complete examples, while the token maximum remains a safety ceiling. Detect truncation explicitly before delivery. A hard cutoff is not a reliable summarization technique because it can remove the very uncertainty statement that makes the answer acceptable.

questions.title: A prefix that can actually repeat
questions.stem: A craft marketplace reuses a long taxonomy and tool definitions across many catalogue-enrichment requests. Each request currently adds a unique request identifier near the start of the system text. Engineers enable prefix caching but see few cache reads. Which TWO changes best address the observed cache behavior while preserving request correlation and avoiding any assumption that cached content changes model quality?

options.text: Keep the reusable tool and taxonomy prefix identical, placing request-specific identifiers and product data after the intended cache boundary.
options.why: A stable prefix supplies the repeated content required for reuse while retaining the dynamic information needed for the individual enrichment task.

options.text: Put a fresh timestamp in every tool description so the cache knows which request has permission to reuse its taxonomy.
options.why: Changing an earlier component of the prefix prevents matching rather than authorizing reuse and is unrelated to application-level access control.

options.text: Correlate requests in application telemetry and compare cache-read and cache-creation usage before and after the prompt reorganization.
options.why: Usage measurements establish whether the intended prefix is being reused; application correlation does not require changing that prefix itself.

options.text: Increase the cache lifetime first because a longer lifetime makes different request identifiers compare as equivalent cache keys.
options.why: A longer lifetime cannot turn nonidentical prefixes into matches; it addresses expiration rather than the demonstrated source of prefix variation.

options.text: Remove product-specific fields from the entire request so every catalogue item receives exactly the same prompt and cached completion.
options.why: Prefix caching reuses processing of common input, not a universal answer; removing item data would undermine the enrichment task itself.

questions.decision: Cache reuse depends on a matching prefix. Keep shared tools and taxonomy stable before the breakpoint, and move changing request data later. Verify the expected reuse through usage fields. Correlation remains important, but a request identifier need not perturb the common model prefix merely to appear in application telemetry.

questions.title: A skill as an entry point
questions.stem: A conservation charity maintains field-reporting procedures for six habitats. Every procedure shares a small triage checklist, but most species tables are needed only for one habitat. Staff use the same agent for unrelated administrative tasks. Which design BEST makes procedures discoverable and maintainable while limiting irrelevant context, assuming the skill system supports metadata, an instruction body, and referenced bundled files?

options.text: Keep clear triggering metadata and a compact shared workflow, with habitat-specific tables in referenced files loaded when the procedure needs them.
options.why: The structure preserves discoverability and common guidance while deferring large reference material that most tasks do not need.

options.text: Create a separate always-loaded skill for every species row so the agent can compare all reference values before choosing a habitat.
options.why: Always loading all rows defeats progressive disclosure and increases selection burden without reflecting the procedure’s shared workflow and habitat structure.

options.text: Paste every habitat table into the agent’s permanent system instructions so administrators never need to maintain referenced files.
options.why: Permanent loading adds irrelevant material to unrelated work and does not eliminate maintenance; it merely concentrates it in the shared prompt.

options.text: Move the entire triage checklist into an unnamed attachment and rely on the model to discover when it should open it.
options.why: An unnamed attachment lacks the explicit discovery cues and entry-point instructions needed to select and apply the procedure reliably.

questions.decision: Use the skill as an entry point that identifies when the procedure applies, carries the compact shared workflow, and references habitat-specific material on demand. Progressive disclosure reduces irrelevant context but does not remove the need for clear descriptions, trustworthy files, and evaluation of whether the right procedure is selected.

video_evidence.concept: A skill as an entry point

questions.title: Remove a capability, preserve the job
questions.stem: A nature reserve agent generates a daily animal-movement digest from a tracking service. The integration exposes a general SQL executor only because the original developer used one fixed read query. The service account can also modify tracking records. The digest must remain read-only even when a retrieved field note contains hostile instructions. Which TWO changes most directly reduce the unnecessary capability?

options.text: Replace arbitrary SQL execution with a parameterized movement-summary operation that accepts only the required reserve and date range.
options.why: A narrow interface removes unrelated query capability while still supporting the exact daily-digest operation the agent must perform.

options.text: Add discovery so the SQL executor is absent from the initial prompt while keeping it discoverable for every reserve request.
options.why: Deferred exposure saves context but does not remove the capability or restrict the executor’s authority when it is discovered.

options.text: Keep writable credentials because a read-only tool description makes them unreachable under every possible injected field-note instruction.
options.why: Descriptions are not authorization controls, and the broad credential remains capable of modifications if any execution path reaches it.

options.text: Use database credentials restricted to the required read views, independently of the tool description and the model’s instructions.
options.why: Underlying authorization limits what can happen even if a tool-selection or argument-validation boundary fails during an adversarial interaction.

options.text: Retain the general executor but rename it read_only_summary so the model reliably understands that record changes are prohibited.
options.why: A name communicates intention but does not remove write authority or prevent arbitrary SQL from reaching the underlying database service.

questions.decision: Reduce the interface and the underlying authority together. A fixed read operation prevents arbitrary query construction, while read-only credentials limit damage if another interface path fails. Search or prompt instructions can improve selection, but neither withdraws the write capability available through a general executor.

video_evidence.concept: Remove a capability, preserve the job

questions.title: Consolidate semantics, retain boundaries
questions.stem: A research catalogue exposes separate tools called search_records, find_entries, locate_items, and query_catalogue. Their documented behavior and access scope are identical, but they return differently named versions of the same fields. Traces show repeated calls with identical queries. Which interface change BEST reduces selection confusion without combining operations that actually have different authorization requirements or business meaning?

options.text: Randomly select an alias in application code and retain all result shapes, making repeated agent calls appear more diverse.
options.why: Random alias selection does not establish a canonical contract and leaves clients and the model handling equivalent results inconsistently.

options.text: Merge catalogue search and catalogue deletion into a single general operation so the agent learns only one available tool name.
options.why: Reducing names by merging different authority boundaries would expand the read use case into an unnecessary write capability.

options.text: Keep all aliases and add a fifth chooser tool that selects which equivalent search tool should receive every request.
options.why: The extra chooser preserves the redundant surface and adds another decision without a meaningful semantic distinction to resolve.

options.text: Provide one documented catalogue-search contract with canonical result fields, retiring redundant aliases after validating representative client and agent queries.
options.why: The tools are semantically equivalent, so consolidation removes accidental choice and result-shape ambiguity without broadening the catalogue operation.

questions.decision: Consolidate genuinely equivalent behavior behind one clear contract and migrate the aliases. The goal is to remove accidental overlap, not force all operations into a general-purpose executor. Validate the new tool description on representative queries and keep distinct operations separate when their semantics or authority differ.

questions.title: Bind authorization to the destination
questions.stem: A remote archive MCP service accepts OAuth tokens. During integration testing, the service accepts a token issued for an unrelated image API because both use the same identity provider. The team is reviewing the published MCP authorization contract before launch. Which TWO controls address this destination-confusion risk at the client and resource-server boundaries? The service remains in staging during review.

options.text: Allow every correctly signed token from the identity provider because a shared issuer proves that all service audiences are equivalent.
options.why: Issuer trust verifies one aspect of a token but does not establish that its intended audience includes this particular MCP service.

options.text: Have the client include the intended MCP resource indicator in authorization and token requests according to the selected protocol specification.
options.why: The resource indicator identifies the destination for which authorization is being requested instead of treating tokens as interchangeable across services.

options.text: Ask the model to inspect the bearer token before calling the tool and explain whether its destination appears appropriate.
options.why: Tokens should stay outside model context, and model interpretation cannot replace deterministic validation at the protected resource boundary.

options.text: Rename the MCP tool to include the archive hostname while retaining the existing issuer-only token validation in server code.
options.why: Tool naming does not change the token’s audience or repair the service’s acceptance of credentials issued for an unrelated resource.

options.text: Have the MCP service validate token audience and reject tokens that were not specifically issued for that protected resource.
options.why: Resource-server audience validation prevents a token trusted by the same identity provider from being reused at an unintended service.

questions.decision: MCP authorization separates identity-provider trust from token audience. The client names the intended resource when requesting authorization and tokens; the server validates that a presented token was issued for it. A valid signature alone does not establish permission to use a token at an unrelated protected service.

questions.title: A local process still has secrets
questions.stem: A local stdio MCP process helps chemists query a proprietary materials catalogue. The catalogue requires a credential, but the local transport does not use the remote HTTP OAuth flow. Developers propose embedding the credential in a tool description so it travels with every request. Which approach BEST separates local transport configuration from downstream authorization and the model’s data context?

options.text: Provide the scoped catalogue credential through protected process configuration, keep it out of model context, and redact it from tool telemetry.
options.why: The transport and downstream service have different credential needs; protected configuration supports the local process without exposing secrets in descriptions.

options.text: Implement an HTTP OAuth callback inside every tool invocation even though the client and server use only local stdio transport.
options.why: The remote authorization flow is not required by this transport and does not justify exposing or repeatedly negotiating the downstream catalogue credential.

options.text: Put the catalogue credential in the tool description but instruct the model to include it only in valid catalogue requests.
options.why: The description enters model context and creates unnecessary leakage risk, while the instruction cannot enforce the intended secret-handling boundary.

options.text: Remove catalogue authentication because a stdio MCP connection establishes authorization to every downstream service the local process can reach.
options.why: Local transport does not confer rights at the proprietary catalogue, whose credential requirement remains independently applicable to the process.

questions.decision: A local process can receive its downstream credential through an appropriate protected configuration channel without placing it in model-visible descriptions. The absence of HTTP MCP OAuth does not make downstream APIs anonymous. Limit the catalogue credential to the required scope and avoid leaking it through traces or returned tool results.

video_evidence.concept: A local process still has secrets

questions.title: Pay for useful retrieval
questions.stem: A patent landscape assistant compares two retrieval configurations on the same held-out query set. Configuration A retrieves six chunks; B retrieves twenty. The exhibit includes generation and retrieval together. The owner requires evidence coverage of at least 92% and p95 latency no greater than 3.0 seconds. Which choice is supported by the measurements without assuming that more retrieved material is inherently better?

options.text: Average A and B’s latency values and deploy both equally because the resulting arithmetic average satisfies the p95 contract.
options.why: Averaging configuration percentiles does not establish the percentile of a traffic mixture or prove the required user-visible tail behavior.

options.text: Use B and lower the generation output cap until end-to-end p95 must fall below the required three-second threshold.
options.why: An output cap is an unmeasured change that can truncate answers; the exhibit does not prove it repairs latency while preserving coverage.

options.text: Retain A for the current contract and investigate targeted retrieval improvements separately using the same coverage and latency acceptance gates.
options.why: A satisfies both requirements, while the larger retrieval configuration misses the independently binding latency limit despite its small coverage gain.

options.text: Adopt B because its higher evidence coverage makes its measured latency irrelevant for a research-oriented product like this assistant.
options.why: The owner explicitly defined a latency gate, so the product category does not authorize replacing it with an accuracy-only decision.

questions.decision: A meets the coverage and latency gates and costs less per request. B improves measured coverage slightly but fails the latency limit, so it is not feasible under the current contract. The result supports A for this workload; it does not establish that six chunks is a universal retrieval optimum.

questions.title: Carry causality through the queue
questions.stem: A flood-report assistant accepts uploads, queues extraction work, and later assembles a response from two workers. Traces end at queue publication; extraction spans look like unrelated jobs. Matching timestamps becomes unreliable during storms, when many uploads arrive together. Which TWO instrumentation changes best establish causal request visibility while avoiding sensitive document content in the tracing headers?

options.text: Infer parent-child relationships from identical model names because workers using the same model usually belong to the same uploaded report.
options.why: Model identity is shared across many jobs and does not establish causal association between a particular upload and a worker execution.

options.text: Inject trace context into queue metadata and extract it when workers create the corresponding processing spans for each upload.
options.why: Explicit propagation connects asynchronous work to its initiating request rather than relying on timestamps that collide under storm-driven concurrency.

options.text: Copy the uploaded report into a tracing header so every downstream observer can identify its request by matching document text.
options.why: Sensitive content is unnecessary for correlation and may leak widely through infrastructure that records or forwards trace metadata.

options.text: Record job identifiers, stage outcomes, and relevant configuration versions while keeping documents and credentials outside propagated tracing headers.
options.why: These attributes support diagnosis and attribution without turning cross-service metadata into a transport for sensitive content or live authentication secrets.

options.text: Assign every worker a new unrelated trace and group charts by the hour, since asynchronous processing cannot preserve upstream causality.
options.why: Asynchronous boundaries can propagate context; hourly grouping loses individual causal relationships and cannot reliably reconstruct overlapping requests at peak volume.

questions.decision: Propagate trace context through the queue and link worker spans to the correct upstream operation. Attach stable versions and nonsecret identifiers so investigators can explain a request’s path. Timing proximity and copied content are poor substitutes for explicit causality, especially when many jobs overlap during peak demand.

questions.title: An index needs a withdrawal path
questions.stem: A music-rights assistant retrieves licensing notes from both a lexical index and a vector index. Rights owners can withdraw a note immediately, while archive copies remain under separate legal retention rules and are excluded from answers. The current ingestion job processes additions and edits only. Which change BEST prevents withdrawn notes from supporting new answers while preserving the stipulated archive policy?

options.text: Delete every archival copy immediately because removing a serving index entry necessarily determines the legal retention of the original document.
options.why: Serving eligibility and the stipulated archival obligation are separate; the scenario does not authorize overriding the archive’s approved retention policy.

options.text: Retain the note in both serving indexes but reduce its vector similarity score so newer licensing notes normally outrank it.
options.why: A ranking adjustment leaves the withdrawn note retrievable and cannot guarantee exclusion from lexical results or uncommon user queries.

options.text: Add an instruction to ignore withdrawn notes without passing withdrawal identifiers or changing either index’s existing searchable records.
options.why: The model lacks reliable withdrawal evidence, and a prompt rule does not remove disallowed documents from the serving retrieval path.

options.text: Track document withdrawal state and propagate removals to all serving indexes and caches, verifying that new retrievals exclude the note.
options.why: This enforces the answer-serving boundary while allowing the separately governed archive to follow its stipulated legal retention policy.

questions.decision: Withdrawal must propagate through every serving index and cache with a testable state transition. Keeping an archival copy under a separate approved policy does not authorize its use for answers. The serving path needs document identity and status so removal is verifiable across retrieval methods rather than dependent on similarity ranking.

video_evidence.concept: An index needs a withdrawal path

questions.title: Preserve the meaning of a table
questions.stem: A horticultural research assistant answers questions from trial tables containing cultivar, irrigation level, yield, confidence interval, and growing season. A plain-text export interleaves values from adjacent columns; retrieval finds the right trial but the generated comparison assigns intervals to the wrong cultivar. Which TWO ingestion changes best address the structural failure before experimenting with a more capable generation model?

options.text: Increase overlap between flattened text chunks while leaving the export’s interleaved column order unchanged across all trial documents.
options.why: Overlap can preserve nearby text but cannot restore reliable row-column relationships that the export has already failed to represent.

options.text: Validate representative extracted rows against the original tables and retain source coordinates so an answer can be audited against the trial.
options.why: Extraction checks establish whether the evidence itself is correct, and source coordinates support later verification of generated comparisons.

options.text: Convert every numeric value into its own embedding record without a cultivar or column label so retrieval becomes more precise.
options.why: A value without its labels and units loses the very semantic association required for the cultivar comparison in this workload.

options.text: Retrieve the entire research archive for every comparison so the generator can infer missing table relationships from other seasons.
options.why: Unrelated archive context adds cost and noise without verifying the lost associations in the particular table supporting the requested comparison.

options.text: Extract table records with column names, units, cultivar identity, and trial-season metadata attached to each retrievable row or coherent group.
options.why: This preserves the associations needed to interpret values rather than presenting an undifferentiated sequence of numbers from adjacent columns.

questions.decision: The information must remain correctly associated before retrieval can ground a comparison. Preserve row-column relationships and trial metadata, then verify extraction against representative tables. Increasing model capacity or chunk overlap cannot reliably reconstruct relationships already lost in the export, particularly when neighboring rows contain similar numeric values.

video_evidence.concept: Preserve the meaning of a table

questions.title: Exact constraints plus meaning
questions.stem: A historic-building procurement assistant must find stone replacement stock. Requests combine a compressive-strength minimum, a delivery region, available quantity, and a description such as warm grey with fine grain. Inventory stores the numeric constraints as typed fields and appearance as prose. Which retrieval plan BEST treats contractual constraints differently from aesthetic similarity while keeping explanations tied to actual available stock?

options.text: Filter typed strength, region, and quantity fields first, then rank the eligible records semantically using the appearance description.
options.why: The plan enforces contractual constraints independently and uses semantic retrieval for the genuinely descriptive portion of the stock request.

options.text: Search the exact phrase warm grey with fine grain in every numeric inventory field and return the closest lexical match.
options.why: The phrase belongs to descriptive prose, while numeric eligibility requires typed comparisons rather than literal matching against unrelated fields.

options.text: Generate a synthetic ideal stock record from the request and send it directly to procurement without querying current inventory availability.
options.why: A generated ideal record is not evidence that purchasable stock exists or satisfies the required contractual constraints in the inventory.

options.text: Search appearance embeddings only and ask the model to infer whether highly similar stock probably meets the minimum strength requirement.
options.why: Appearance similarity does not establish a numeric strength guarantee or available quantity, leaving the contractual eligibility conditions unenforced.

questions.decision: Apply the hard inventory constraints using typed queries, then rank eligible records by appearance relevance and return their identifiers. A semantic score is useful for the descriptive preference but cannot certify numeric thresholds or quantity availability. The generator should explain retrieved candidates rather than invent availability from prose resemblance.

questions.title: Restore a follow-up’s referent
questions.stem: A theatre archive assistant answers a question about a director’s productions in a particular decade. The next user message is “Which of those toured abroad?” Retrieval using only that sentence returns general touring advice. The conversation includes the relevant director and time range, but the index has no conversation memory. Which approach BEST restores query meaning while preserving authorization filters on archive records?

options.text: Retrieve on the follow-up alone with a much larger top-k so all potentially related international touring information reaches the model.
options.why: More results from an underspecified query add unrelated material and do not reliably recover the omitted director and decade constraints.

options.text: Rewrite the follow-up with the director, decade, and touring criterion from context, then retrieve under the user’s existing access filters.
options.why: The rewritten query supplies the missing referents while preserving authorization and grounding the response in the relevant archive records.

options.text: Reuse the first answer as the sole evidence because a conversation summary has already established which productions were relevant.
options.why: The first answer may omit touring details or contain errors; it does not replace retrieval of the records needed for the new criterion.

options.text: Rewrite the follow-up with archive-wide access so the model sees enough productions to identify which ones the user probably intended.
options.why: Query clarification does not authorize broader access, and additional unauthorized records are unnecessary for restoring the conversation’s known referents.

questions.decision: Resolve the follow-up into a standalone retrieval query that retains the named subject and constraints from the conversation. Continue applying the same access filters and ground the answer in actual retrieved production records. A larger top-k cannot fix a query whose referents and time range are missing.

questions.title: Choose the boundary, not the fashion
questions.stem: A coastal engineering firm needs tidal-risk maps from a partner. The partner offers a deterministic elevation lookup API and a separate planning agent that investigates local scenarios using private modelling expertise. Your application needs both a precise elevation value and a reasoned scenario assessment. Which TWO integration choices best match the two distinct responsibilities without implying that any external service is automatically an autonomous agent?

options.text: Delegate the scenario assessment through a bounded partner-agent contract specifying scope, evidence, completion status, and allowed turnaround time.
options.why: The partner’s autonomous reasoning and private expertise justify a delegation boundary whose result still needs an explicit application contract.

options.text: Replace the partner’s investigation with a prompt containing only its API documentation because instructions supply the partner’s private modelling expertise.
options.why: Documentation describes interfaces but does not reproduce the partner’s private evidence or expertise needed for the requested scenario assessment.

options.text: Expose both services through one unrestricted shell command so the application avoids defining separate contracts for data and reasoned assessments.
options.why: A shell erases useful type and authority boundaries and does not remove the need to specify what each external responsibility delivers.

options.text: Use agent-to-agent delegation for the elevation lookup because every operation crossing an organizational boundary requires autonomous negotiation.
options.why: An organizational boundary does not change a deterministic lookup into an autonomous reasoning task or require a more complex integration mechanism.

options.text: Call the elevation API through a typed deterministic client or tool that validates coordinates, units, and returned data identifiers.
options.why: The operation has fixed inputs and outputs, so it does not need autonomous delegation merely because another company operates it.

questions.decision: Integrate deterministic data retrieval as a tool or direct API, and delegate the reasoned investigation through a bounded agent contract when the partner supplies that expertise. The mechanisms can coexist. Ownership, inputs, outputs, time limits, and evidence expectations should be explicit at each boundary rather than inferred from a vendor relationship.

video_evidence.concept: Choose the boundary, not the fashion

questions.title: Discovery must be discoverable
questions.stem: A municipal records assistant has hundreds of specialist read tools behind search. Initial context size falls, but requests about building permits often discover unrelated tools. Several permit tools are described only as handler or utility. Which TWO changes best improve the discovery design while preserving its context advantage and keeping authorization separate from search ranking?

options.text: Treat a tool’s high search rank as permission to access its records because the model selected it for a legitimate question.
options.why: A relevance score does not establish user authorization or record entitlement, which must remain enforced by the execution path.

options.text: Evaluate tool discovery recall on representative permit queries, then separately enforce user and record permissions at execution time.
options.why: Discovery quality and authorization are different controls; measuring one cannot replace enforcement of the other at the serving boundary.

options.text: Write precise tool names and descriptions covering permit tasks, required inputs, return data, and distinctions from similarly named services.
options.why: Search can use meaningful metadata to find the right capability without placing every detailed definition into the initial model context.

options.text: Load every tool permanently because a discovery failure proves that progressive loading can never work for municipal records.
options.why: The observed failure is tied to poor metadata; reverting immediately discards the context benefit without testing the specific discovered cause.

options.text: Shorten all descriptions to one generic word so the search mechanism can compare tools without being distracted by domain terminology.
options.why: Generic descriptions remove the identifying information needed for retrieval and would worsen the tool-selection problem shown in the traces.

questions.decision: Progressive discovery needs descriptive metadata and its own evaluation. Improve the permit tool summaries, test whether relevant tools are retrieved, and retain server-side access controls. Discovery controls which definitions enter context; it does not establish which records a user may access or guarantee that a vague tool can be found.

questions.title: Measure the rare event
questions.stem: A water-quality classifier flags samples requiring further laboratory investigation. In a labeled batch of 1,000 samples, 40 truly require investigation. The classifier flags 50 samples, including 30 of the true cases. The owner requires recall of at least 80% and precision of at least 55%. Which conclusion follows from the exhibit before any deployment decision is made?

options.text: The classifier passes recall at 60% and precision at 75%, so it should be released with an explanation of the reversed metrics.
options.why: The denominators are reversed, and the resulting conclusion neither computes the required metrics correctly nor establishes that both gates pass.

options.text: The classifier passes precision at 60% but fails recall at 75%; investigate a new operating point before release.
options.why: The calculation uses flagged positives for precision and all true positives for recall, respecting the owner’s two independently stated gates.

options.text: The classifier passes both gates because its 97% overall accuracy is greater than either required percentage in the acceptance contract.
options.why: Overall accuracy answers a different question and cannot substitute for the explicitly required positive-class precision and recall thresholds.

options.text: The classifier passes recall at 80% because the ten missed cases represent only one percent of all sampled water.
options.why: The missed cases must be compared with the forty true investigation cases, not diluted by the much larger negative class.

questions.decision: Recall is 30/40 = 75%; precision is 30/50 = 60%. The classifier passes precision and misses recall. Overall accuracy is 970/1,000 = 97%, but that does not satisfy the requirement to find at least 80% of samples needing investigation. Further tuning needs a separately evaluated operating point.

questions.title: Task outcome and security outcome
questions.stem: A specimen-shipping agent creates packaging instructions and a carrier booking. Its evaluation currently grades instruction clarity and whether the final response contains a tracking reference. A valid reference can be generated even when the carrier booking is rejected, and injected shipment notes have occasionally attempted unauthorized address changes. Which TWO additional measurements most directly test the outcomes the existing rubric misses?

options.text: Have the generator self-report whether its address changes were authorized and use that declaration as the sole security label.
options.why: Self-report does not independently establish authorization or show whether the integration enforced the shipment’s actual destination-change boundary.

options.text: Measure only the agent’s mean tool-call count because fewer calls demonstrate that shipping tasks are completed more efficiently.
options.why: Call count is an efficiency measure and can improve when the agent skips the very booking or validation step required for success.

options.text: Increase the weight of tracking-reference formatting because a stricter reference pattern should distinguish rejected bookings from successful carrier transactions.
options.why: A reference’s syntax does not establish carrier acceptance; the scenario explicitly permits a valid-looking reference when the booking fails.

options.text: Verify completed booking state in the carrier’s test system using the requested shipment identity and authorized destination.
options.why: The external state distinguishes a real completed task from a plausible response containing a reference that the carrier never accepted.

options.text: Measure unauthorized destination-change attempts and successful changes on injected notes, including enforcement at the carrier integration boundary.
options.why: The adversarial measurement tests the security requirement directly rather than assuming a clear packaging explanation implies safe execution of shipment actions.

questions.decision: Grade the externally observable task outcome, not merely a convincing completion message, and test unauthorized behavior under adversarial inputs. Both can fail while an answer looks clear and includes a reference. Keep the task’s success definition and its security constraints separately observable so one cannot conceal the other.

questions.title: Calibrate a judge on its blind spot
questions.stem: A film-subtitle evaluation uses a model judge to assess meaning preservation. The judge agrees with experts on fluent translations, but no one has tested fluent subtitles that quietly reverse who performed an action. The team can fund fifty more expert labels. Which use of that budget BEST improves confidence in this judge before scaling automated evaluation to a large subtitle corpus?

options.text: Create matched fluent subtitles with preserved or reversed agency, obtain blinded expert labels, and measure the judge’s ability to distinguish them.
options.why: The challenge set targets the known evaluation gap and tests discrimination rather than extending agreement evidence on already represented easy cases.

options.text: Ask experts to rank the judge’s written explanations for eloquence, retaining the most persuasive explanation style as the calibrated evaluator.
options.why: Persuasive explanations are not a substitute for correct verdicts on semantic failures, so this does not calibrate the intended judgment.

options.text: Average the judge’s scores with the generator’s self-confidence so difficult translations receive a more stable combined evaluation signal.
options.why: Two model-derived signals do not establish correctness without the independent negative examples needed to expose this particular blind spot.

options.text: Spend all fifty labels on additional fluent translations selected by the generator as its strongest examples of meaning preservation.
options.why: This expands the same positive-only evidence and still does not show whether the judge rejects the subtle negative case of reversed agency.

questions.decision: Use the budget to challenge the judge with expert-labeled positive and negative cases around the untested semantic failure. Measure detection and disagreement, then refine the rubric. Agreement on easy fluent outputs does not establish discrimination against fluent but meaning-reversing outputs, regardless of the judge’s eloquent explanations.

video_evidence.concept: Calibrate a judge on its blind spot

questions.title: Three layers of grading
questions.stem: A chemistry education assistant produces a structured molecule identifier, cites a source passage, and explains a reaction at an agreed student level. The team has code checks, expert labels, and a candidate model judge available. It needs scalable evaluation while retaining sensitivity to subtle scientific errors. Which THREE assignments best match the grading method to the evidence it can reliably assess?

options.text: Treat every response with a valid molecule identifier as scientifically correct, using the code validator to replace explanation grading.
options.why: Identifier syntax does not establish reaction correctness or student-level appropriateness, leaving both substantive evaluation requirements unsupported.

options.text: Use code to validate identifier syntax, required fields, and whether cited passage identifiers resolve to the supplied reference corpus.
options.why: These properties have deterministic expected behavior, making code a reliable and scalable grader for the response’s structural and referential checks.

options.text: Calibrate the model judge against expert-labeled explanations, including plausible but scientifically incorrect reactions and unnecessarily advanced language.
options.why: Calibration tests the nuanced judgments needed for scientific fidelity and student appropriateness rather than assuming that fluent explanations are accurate.

options.text: Retain expert-adjudicated challenge cases for subtle scientific failures and periodically audit automated grading disagreements against the agreed rubric.
options.why: Experts provide independent evidence for cases the automated methods may misjudge, while targeted auditing controls cost without abandoning nuanced validation.

options.text: Require the same generator session to grade all explanations from its full drafting context, eliminating differences between author and evaluator.
options.why: Shared author context can reinforce the same assumptions and does not provide independent evidence that the explanation meets the scientific rubric.

questions.decision: Use deterministic checks for deterministic properties, calibrated rubric grading for nuanced explanation, and expert challenge cases where scientific correctness is difficult to automate. These layers complement each other. A valid identifier and citation format do not prove that a cited passage supports the reaction explanation or that the explanation is scientifically sound.

questions.title: Choose the experimental unit
questions.stem: A railway information assistant is comparing two conversation policies. A policy can alter which clarifying question is asked, affecting later turns. Requests are currently randomized independently, so passengers often switch policies during one conversation. Both variants use the same retrieval service. Which experimental redesign BEST permits an interpretable comparison of complete conversational experiences without confounding assignment with the time of day?

options.text: Randomize at conversation start, keep assignment stable through the session, and analyze complete-session outcomes under the predeclared comparison plan.
options.why: The unit matches the policy’s multi-turn effect and avoids contaminating one passenger experience with behavior from both experimental variants.

options.text: Assign all frequent passengers to the established policy and new passengers to the candidate policy so each receives consistent behavior.
options.why: Assignment would be confounded with passenger experience and usage patterns, preventing a clean attribution of outcome differences to the policy.

options.text: Keep per-request randomization but grade only final responses, since earlier clarifying questions are no longer visible in the measured outcome.
options.why: Earlier questions affect later responses and passenger behavior, so excluding them from grading does not remove the mixed-treatment contamination.

options.text: Alternate policies every fifteen minutes and compare daily means because every policy then receives traffic from multiple station rush periods.
options.why: Time blocks can confound policy with changing disruption and demand conditions and still switch sessions that span a block boundary.

questions.decision: Assign the conversation to one policy and retain that assignment for its dependent turns. Analyze conversation outcomes under the assigned policy and account for repeated users if they matter to the hypothesis. Per-turn switching contaminates the treatment, while time-block switching can entangle the policy with changes in demand or disruptions.

questions.title: Learn without moving the finish line
questions.stem: A livestock-record assistant’s candidate prompt underperforms in a preregistered online comparison despite a strong offline result. Investigators find abbreviations and fragmented notes absent from the offline corpus. The experiment has reached its planned endpoint. Which TWO next steps support a defensible iteration rather than selectively searching for a favorable result? The baseline remains available throughout the controlled pilot.

options.text: Continue the completed experiment until the candidate’s cumulative score exceeds the baseline, leaving the original endpoint out of the report.
