options.why: Selective extension changes the decision procedure after observing results and does not fix the underlying representativeness problem in the offline corpus.

options.text: Curate representative abbreviated notes into development evaluations, reserve an independent holdout, and test a focused repair under a new plan.
options.why: This addresses the demonstrated distribution gap while preserving independent evidence for whether the next prompt generalizes to live-style inputs.

options.text: Change the prompt, retrieval engine, and model simultaneously, then attribute any subsequent improvement specifically to the new wording.
options.why: A bundled change may improve outcomes but would not isolate the proposed prompt mechanism or support that specific causal attribution.

options.text: Keep the candidate from general rollout and document the observed loss and the abbreviated-note failure slice from the completed test.
options.why: The online result is relevant evidence about the live workload and should remain visible even when it contradicts the offline result.

options.text: Remove abbreviated notes from online scoring because they were absent from the offline evaluation and therefore outside the candidate’s intended distribution.
options.why: The notes are part of the live workload described by the service; excluding failures would conceal the gap rather than establish readiness.

questions.decision: Use the completed experiment as evidence, diagnose the distribution gap, and improve representativeness before testing a specific repair. Protect a fresh holdout for the next iteration. Repeating the same comparison until a favorable outcome appears would not resolve the missing coverage or support a trustworthy claim of improvement.

video_evidence.concept: Learn without moving the finish line

questions.title: Distinguish retrieval from generation
questions.stem: A restoration-history assistant states that a sculpture was repaired in the wrong year. The trace shows that the retrieved passage clearly gives the correct year, the cited identifier resolves, and the response was not truncated. The same prompt contains two worked examples that merge project start dates with completion dates. Which next diagnostic action BEST targets the strongest evidence before changing retrieval or model tier?

options.text: Increase retrieval top-k because an answer with a wrong date necessarily means the correct historical passage was not sufficiently represented.
options.why: The trace already contains the clear correct passage; more retrieved material does not directly repair the contradictory examples shown in context.

options.text: Extend the output cap because the incorrect year indicates the response probably stopped before it could correct its own first statement.
options.why: The trace rules out truncation, and extra output allowance does not address why the prompt examples conflate two different date meanings.

options.text: Move immediately to a larger model and change the examples later, using the wrong year as evidence of insufficient reasoning capacity.
options.why: Capacity remains a possible factor, but the explicit example conflict is stronger actionable evidence and should be tested before a broader change.

options.text: Correct the examples’ date semantics and rerun matched start-date and completion-date cases while keeping the retrieved evidence and model configuration fixed.
options.why: The proposed change targets the observed instructional conflict and isolates whether that mechanism caused the incorrect year in the generated answer.

questions.decision: The correct evidence already reached the model, and the worked examples teach the observed date conflation. Repair that contradiction first and test matched start/completion cases with retrieval held stable. This is a focused hypothesis, not proof that retrieval or model capacity can never fail elsewhere in the application.

questions.title: Disagreement is a signal, not a verdict
questions.stem: A natural-history summarizer has no full reference summary for each source. The team generates independent summaries and flags claims that differ. A disputed claim about migration dates appears in only one summary. The underlying field report remains available. Which handling BEST uses inconsistency testing without falsely treating agreement or disagreement as a factual guarantee? The verification budget is limited.

options.text: Average the migration dates across summaries and publish the midpoint because numerical aggregation reduces disagreement between independent generations.
options.why: A midpoint can be unsupported by every source and turns differing factual claims into a fabricated value rather than resolving the evidence.

options.text: Flag the disputed migration claim for comparison with the report, recording the supporting passage or removing the unsupported assertion.
options.why: Inconsistency identifies a useful verification target, while the available source supplies the evidence needed to decide whether the claim is supported.

options.text: Delete the minority claim automatically because the number of independent summaries containing a fact establishes whether the fact is true.
options.why: A correct detail may appear in only one summary, and frequency alone does not determine its support in the underlying report.

options.text: Accept every claim shared by all summaries and reserve source checks only for claims generated by the smallest model configuration.
options.why: Agreement can reflect shared systematic errors, and model size does not define which claims need evidence-based verification in the source.

questions.decision: Use inconsistency to prioritize source verification, then resolve the claim against the report. Multiple generations can share an error, and a minority statement can be correct. The technique helps locate suspicious claims but cannot replace evidence checks or establish calibrated correctness from voting alone.

video_evidence.concept: Disagreement is a signal, not a verdict

questions.title: Count the savings that matter
questions.stem: A public-art catalogue assistant currently includes eighteen retrieved passages of 700 tokens in every request. An evaluated reranker keeps seven passages with unchanged answer acceptance on the held-out workload. The reranker itself costs 300 input-equivalent tokens per request under the team’s stipulated accounting. Excluding other unchanged costs, what net input-equivalent reduction does the proposed configuration achieve per request?

options.text: A reduction of 5,200 input-equivalent tokens because seven retained passages and the reranker together define how much was removed.
options.why: Five thousand two hundred is the new accounted input, not the difference between the original and proposed configurations in this calculation.

options.text: A reduction of 12,300 input-equivalent tokens because reranking replaces retrieval context rather than selecting passages for the final answer.
options.why: The proposed pipeline still sends seven passages, so the calculation must include their four thousand nine hundred tokens alongside the reranker charge.

options.text: A reduction of 7,700 input-equivalent tokens because the reranker is not part of the final generation prompt and therefore has no cost.
options.why: The team explicitly includes the reranker’s three hundred token-equivalent charge, so omitting it overstates the net saving under the given accounting.

options.text: A reduction of 7,400 input-equivalent tokens, with release quality gates and measured end-to-end latency retained for the changed pipeline.
options.why: The calculation subtracts both retained context and the stipulated reranker charge from the original context instead of ignoring the new stage’s cost.

questions.decision: The original retrieval context is 18 × 700 = 12,600 tokens. The new context plus reranker charge is 7 × 700 + 300 = 5,200 token equivalents, yielding a reduction of 7,400. The quality result is workload-specific; retain release gates and measure live latency before claiming a production benefit.

questions.title: Observe the journey and the revision
questions.stem: A ceramic-repair advisory assistant has healthy request latency but conservators increasingly abandon sessions after repeated clarifying questions. The issue begins after a prompt revision and is concentrated in uploaded handwritten reports. Which TWO monitoring additions best reveal the regression and connect it to a repair hypothesis without treating an HTTP success as evidence of a useful conversation?

options.text: Use the mean response length as the primary completion metric because repeated clarifying questions tend to make conversations longer.
options.why: Response length is an indirect proxy and cannot distinguish necessary clarification from a session that fails to resolve the conservator’s actual problem.

options.text: Track only total monthly sessions because stable demand would demonstrate that conservators still find the revised assistant useful.
options.why: Traffic volume can remain stable while users abandon individual consultations, so it does not measure the failed outcome described in the scenario.

options.text: Break those outcomes down by report type and prompt version, retaining correlated stage traces for representative failing and successful sessions.
options.why: The breakdown can localize the regression and support comparison against a baseline rather than presenting an undifferentiated overall success rate.

options.text: Combine all prompt versions and report types into one rolling average to obtain a stable signal before investigating individual complaints.
options.why: Aggregation would conceal the concentrated revision-specific failure and weaken the team’s ability to identify the input slice and mechanism involved.

options.text: Track session completion, abandonment, repeated-question patterns, and turns to useful resolution under a consistently defined consultation outcome.
options.why: These signals describe the user journey that request latency and successful API responses fail to capture in this multi-turn service.

questions.decision: Monitor session outcomes and their distribution across input type and configuration version. This connects user-visible abandonment with the changed prompt and handwritten-report slice. Request metrics remain useful for infrastructure health, but they do not show whether a multi-turn consultation reached a useful outcome or became stuck in clarification.

video_evidence.concept: Observe the journey and the revision

questions.title: Constrain a fetch beyond its hostname
questions.stem: A manuscript-research agent fetches external catalogues through an allowlisted domain. A security test finds that the domain redirects to a private network address, which the fetcher follows. The domain owner may also change DNS responses between validation and connection. Which TWO controls best strengthen the actual network boundary while preserving access to permitted public catalogues?

options.text: Keep hostname validation and add a prompt rule against private addresses, relying on the model to inspect each redirect before following it.
options.why: The fetcher follows redirects below the model’s decision layer, so a prompt rule cannot enforce the actual network destination boundary.

options.text: Allow redirects whenever the first URL uses HTTPS because encrypted transport establishes that every later destination is a public catalogue.
options.why: Encryption protects transport but does not establish the public-network eligibility or intended identity of a subsequent redirect destination.

options.text: Route fetching through an egress boundary that blocks internal and metadata destinations independently of any instructions present in retrieved catalogue text.
options.why: Network enforcement limits reachable destinations even if an injected document persuades the agent to issue a fetch that bypasses its intended research behavior.

options.text: Cache the first DNS result for the entire month and remove other validation to make subsequent catalogue requests consistent.
options.why: A cached result does not validate redirect targets or establish continued safety, and removing enforcement leaves other private-destination paths available.

options.text: Validate redirect targets and resolved destinations against private-address restrictions for each connection, including DNS-change and redirect test cases.
options.why: The identified bypass occurs after the initial hostname check, so validation must cover the destination actually contacted throughout the fetch sequence.

questions.decision: Validate the destination actually contacted, including redirects and resolved addresses, and enforce egress restrictions independently of model behavior. A hostname allowlist alone can miss redirection and DNS rebinding. The control must apply at connection time and across the fetch path, with tests covering the routes that bypassed the initial check.

video_evidence.concept: Constrain a fetch beyond its hostname

questions.title: A path check needs a filesystem model
questions.stem: A microscopy agent may write analysis files only within its job directory. A pre-tool check rejects paths whose text does not start with that directory, but a test writes through a symbolic link inside the directory to an outside file. Shell execution is also enabled for analysis tools. Which control design BEST addresses the stated boundary across those execution routes?

options.text: Reject only paths containing two dots and retain the symbolic-link behavior because the attempted path remains lexically inside the directory.
options.why: Traversal syntax is only one bypass route; the demonstrated symbolic link can reach an outside target without containing two dots.

options.text: Enforce the job directory through filesystem isolation and safe path resolution, covering file tools and shell writes with symlink and traversal tests.
options.why: The design addresses both the observed filesystem indirection and alternate execution route rather than relying on a textual path-prefix comparison alone.

options.text: Apply the hook only to the file-write tool and ask shell-based analysis commands to respect the same directory in their instructions.
options.why: The shell remains another write path, so an unenforced instruction cannot establish the stated boundary across all enabled execution routes.

options.text: Strengthen the prefix check by requiring the directory name twice in every filename, while keeping the existing symbolic links available.
options.why: Repeating a directory string does not change how the filesystem resolves symbolic links or restrict writes performed through shell execution.

questions.decision: A textual prefix test is insufficient when filesystem resolution and alternative tools can bypass it. Enforce the write boundary through filesystem isolation and safe resolved-path handling across all enabled execution routes. Test symbolic links and traversal explicitly; a hook can contribute checks but is not a universal sandbox by itself.

video_evidence.concept: A path check needs a filesystem model

questions.title: Bound an expensive public operation
questions.stem: A citizen-science service lets users ask an agent to analyze uploaded audio. A single request can spawn many classification calls, and authenticated accounts can submit concurrently. The owner accepts partial results when a per-project processing allowance is exhausted. Which THREE controls together best address cost abuse without assuming that authentication, caching, or shorter final answers alone bound the work performed?

options.text: Enforce per-job classification-call and elapsed-time limits, returning completed evidence and explicit partial status when those bounds are reached.
options.why: Inner execution limits prevent an accepted request from expanding without bounds and preserve useful results under the owner’s allowed degraded-service contract.

options.text: Reserve shared processing allowance atomically for concurrent jobs so simultaneous submissions cannot each spend the same remaining project budget.
options.why: Atomic reservation addresses concurrent accounting, preventing individually reasonable jobs from collectively exceeding the project’s enforceable allowance.

options.text: Rely on user login and a published acceptable-use notice because identified users cannot generate unbounded classification cost through valid requests.
options.why: Authentication and terms establish identity and expectations but do not technically constrain request frequency, concurrent jobs, or work expanded within a job.

options.text: Cap the final explanation at one hundred words because a short response limits the total number of hidden classification calls needed.
options.why: Final output length does not reliably bound upstream worker fanout or tool use, which are the expensive operations identified in the scenario.

options.text: Apply account and project admission limits before expensive analysis starts, with an explicit response when a request exceeds the allowed envelope.
options.why: Admission controls bound incoming demand before processing costs accrue and make rejected or deferred requests observable to callers and operators.

questions.decision: Bound demand admission, reserve shared project resources, and constrain work inside each accepted job. These operate at different levels and together cover concurrency and expansion. Authentication identifies an account; it does not limit resource consumption. Cached prefixes and concise output may reduce cost but cannot establish an enforceable upper bound on job fanout.

questions.title: Keep demonstrations outside tenant memory
questions.stem: A ceramics wholesaler uses example quotations to teach an assistant how to write negotiated offers. The examples include another customer’s confidential discount schedule. The retrieval service correctly filters live documents by tenant, but the shared examples are inserted after that filter. Which TWO changes most directly address the resulting leakage path without confusing model-version controls with access isolation?

options.text: Pin the current model version because stable model behavior prevents another tenant’s quotation from appearing in any response.
options.why: Version stability does not remove confidential examples from context or establish an access boundary around information the model can already read.

options.text: Replace shared quotations with reviewed synthetic or appropriately de-identified examples that preserve the writing lesson without exposing another customer’s terms.
options.why: The shared example source itself contains confidential data, so repairing that source closes a path untouched by live retrieval filtering.

options.text: Include shared prompts and examples in tenant-isolation tests, attempting to elicit confidential terms through direct questions and injected document instructions.
options.why: Testing the complete context-assembly path can reveal leakage from sources outside the retrieval filter rather than assuming that component covers everything.

options.text: Add citations to every generated discount because attributing another customer’s confidential terms makes their disclosure transparent and therefore permitted.
options.why: Attribution does not authorize disclosure, and citing the confidential terms would expose their provenance without correcting the cross-tenant leakage.

options.text: Expand the live-document tenant filter to more vector dimensions while leaving the confidential shared quotation examples unchanged after retrieval.
options.why: The leakage path bypasses retrieval entirely, so changing vector filtering does not remove the sensitive examples inserted later in context assembly.

questions.decision: Access isolation must cover all context sources, including shared examples rather than just retrieved documents. Replace confidential examples with reviewed synthetic material and test adversarial attempts to recover other tenants’ information. A correctly filtered retrieval service cannot protect sensitive data independently injected into the prompt after filtering.

questions.title: A useful reviewer can challenge evidence
questions.stem: A mine-safety assistant drafts inspection findings for a qualified engineer. Engineers remain responsible for disposition. The review screen shows a polished summary and an accept button, while measurements, missing observations, and unresolved conflicts sit in a separate system. Reviewers frequently accept an incomplete finding. Which redesign BEST supports meaningful human validation of the assistant’s actual evidence rather than merely adding another approval click?

options.text: Hide the initial recommendation until the engineer submits a disposition, but keep the measurements and unresolved conflicts in the separate system.
options.why: Blind review may reduce anchoring, but the proposed design still withholds the evidence needed to assess completeness at the decision point.

options.text: Show the assistant’s self-reported confidence in large type so engineers can focus only on findings assigned a low confidence value.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence is not a reliable proxy for missing evidence and does not expose the measurements or conflicts needed for substantive validation.

options.text: Present the proposed finding with linked measurements, missing observations, conflicts, and editable disposition; evaluate whether engineers catch known incomplete cases.
options.why: The design supports an informed challenge to the recommendation and measures review effectiveness instead of treating the presence of an approval button as sufficient.

options.text: Require two accept clicks on the same summary, making the second confirmation evidence that the engineer considered the missing observations.
options.why: A repeated click provides no additional evidence and leaves the information necessary for informed review outside the engineer’s immediate decision context.

questions.decision: A reviewer needs the evidence and missing information that determine whether the recommendation is justified. Present provenance, conflicts, and uncertainty alongside a clear disposition mechanism, then audit whether review catches seeded or naturally occurring errors. Human responsibility alone does not make a summary-only approval screen an effective control.

video_evidence.concept: A useful reviewer can challenge evidence

questions.title: Calibrate the people, then measure them
questions.stem: A volunteer ecology programme asks specialists to review species identifications that the assistant marks uncertain. Specialists disagree frequently about juvenile specimens, but agree on adult specimens. The owner wants a defensible review process rather than choosing whichever reviewer accepts more results. Which intervention BEST distinguishes ambiguous evidence from inconsistent interpretation of the review policy? Adult-specimen review remains unchanged.

options.text: Assign every juvenile specimen to the reviewer with the highest acceptance rate so the programme applies a consistent operational threshold.
options.why: Acceptance rate alone does not establish correct interpretation and can systematically favor leniency without resolving ambiguity in juvenile evidence.

options.text: Require specialists to see the assistant’s proposed label before reviewing every juvenile specimen, using agreement with that label as the target.
options.why: Agreement with the generator can reinforce its errors and does not independently establish that reviewers applied the intended evidential standard.

options.text: Average the reviewers’ categorical species labels and return the most common genus without changing the review instructions or auditing disagreements.
options.why: Aggregation does not diagnose why reviewers disagree or establish that a generalized label satisfies the programme’s actual identification requirement.

options.text: Calibrate specialists on juvenile examples with explicit evidence criteria and an unresolved outcome, then measure agreement and audited accuracy by specimen type.
options.why: This separates policy interpretation from genuinely insufficient evidence and checks whether agreement corresponds to correct, useful review outcomes for the difficult slice.

questions.decision: Create a shared juvenile-specimen rubric and calibrate reviewers on independently labeled examples, retaining an unresolved category for genuinely insufficient evidence. Measure agreement by specimen type and audit outcomes. Consensus pressure can hide ambiguity; the objective is a reproducible, useful review policy rather than mechanically maximizing agreement.

video_evidence.concept: Calibrate the people, then measure them

questions.title: Minimize across every copy
questions.stem: Counsel has confirmed that GDPR applies to an EU heritage-membership assistant and approved a narrow purpose: recommend events using declared interests and a preferred city. The context builder also sends birth dates and full street addresses. Engineers propose encrypting those extra fields and keeping them in diagnostic traces. Which response BEST implements the confirmed purpose and data-minimization obligation without making the architect determine the lawful basis?

options.text: Use pseudonyms for member names and keep all other fields because pseudonymization removes every GDPR obligation from the resulting records.
options.why: Pseudonymization does not necessarily make data anonymous, and it does not erase the confirmed minimization obligation for unnecessary personal fields.

options.text: Ask the model to ignore extra profile fields while retaining them for possible future personalization, since future usefulness establishes present necessity.
options.why: A speculative future use does not make the fields necessary for the approved current purpose, and ignoring them does not prevent their processing.

options.text: Remove unneeded birth dates and street addresses from model input and diagnostics, preserving only fields justified by the counsel-approved recommendation purpose.
options.why: The implementation limits processing to the confirmed purpose across both inference and telemetry rather than substituting encryption for necessity.

options.text: Keep the additional fields encrypted in traces because encryption automatically satisfies data minimization even when the recommendation never needs them.
options.why: Encryption safeguards stored data but does not establish that collecting and retaining unnecessary personal fields is justified for the stated purpose.

questions.decision: Under the stipulated scope, unnecessary fields should be removed from the processing path, including diagnostics. Encryption is useful protection but does not make unnecessary personal data necessary. Counsel owns the legal determination; the architect implements the agreed purpose through field selection, logging controls, and verification across all derived copies.

questions.title: Retention is implemented, not implied
questions.stem: Counsel has confirmed that GDPR applies to a community-energy assistant’s identifiable conversations. The controller has approved a ninety-day operational purpose and determined that no exception or legal hold applies to the covered copies. The data appears in an object store, searchable index, and support exports. Which architecture BEST implements the stipulated retention decision rather than treating a storage setting as the whole compliance programme?

options.text: Keep all copies until an individual requests erasure because the right to erasure replaces the controller’s need for a retention schedule.
options.why: A request mechanism does not replace the separately confirmed storage-limitation implementation, and the controller has already established the covered retention period.

options.text: Track covered copies and deletion propagation, expire or genuinely anonymize them at ninety days, and verify the index and export outcomes.
options.why: The design implements the controller’s stated scope across all identified storage paths rather than assuming that one primary-object setting governs derived copies.

options.text: Enable a ninety-day lifecycle rule only on the object store because search indexes and support exports are merely operational metadata.
options.why: The scenario identifies those copies as covered identifiable conversations, so excluding them would leave the approved retention decision incompletely implemented.

options.text: Replace member identifiers with reversible codes and retain the conversations indefinitely because every coded record is legally anonymous by definition.
options.why: Reversible coding is not necessarily anonymization, and indefinite retention contradicts the explicitly stipulated purpose and absence of applicable exceptions.

questions.decision: Implement the controller’s scoped retention rule across the actual data lifecycle and verify that covered copies expire or become genuinely anonymous. The ninety-day period comes from the stipulated owner decision, not from a universal GDPR duration. Indexes and support exports remain relevant copies even when the primary object has been removed.

questions.title: A fair result needs a visible route
questions.stem: A regional arts programme uses an assistant to suggest grant-review summaries; people make the decisions. Applicants writing in regional dialects receive more unsupported negative characterizations than matched standard-language applications. The programme has confirmed that writing dialect is irrelevant to the funded criteria. Which TWO changes best address the measured fairness issue and applicants’ ability to understand or challenge the resulting review process?

options.text: Preserve the negative characterizations but hide AI involvement because applicants may overreact to an automated contribution to a human decision.
options.why: Concealment does not correct unsupported characterizations and weakens applicants’ understanding of the review process and their ability to challenge inaccurate evidence.

options.text: Evaluate matched applications across dialect variants, inspect unsupported characterizations, and validate a repair against the same funding-criterion rubric.
options.why: Matched comparisons target the observed irrelevant-language effect and provide evidence that the repair improves the actual review criterion rather than its tone alone.

options.text: Remove applicants’ names and declare the issue resolved because every dialect cue disappears when direct identity fields are omitted.
options.why: The observed signal is writing dialect, which remains in the application text after names are removed and still needs direct evaluation.

options.text: Provide applicants an accessible explanation of the assistant’s role, relevant criteria, limitations, and a route to contest inaccurate review evidence.
options.why: The explanation and challenge route let applicants understand and correct the process without assuming that a human signature alone makes it transparent.

options.text: Publish the complete system prompt as the sole explanation, without describing funding criteria or how applicants can contest factual mistakes.
options.why: Raw implementation text does not necessarily provide an accessible account of the process, its limits, or the available route to correct errors.

questions.decision: Use matched evidence to test whether dialect changes irrelevant judgments, and explain how AI contributes to the review with a meaningful challenge route. Human final decisions do not automatically remove upstream framing bias. Transparency should describe criteria and limits in applicant language rather than expose raw prompts without an understandable account.

video_evidence.concept: A fair result needs a visible route

questions.title: Discover the last-mile workflow
questions.stem: A veterinary records assistant has promising extraction accuracy on scanned referral letters. Discovery interviewed the software team and clinic managers but did not observe receptionists who reconcile records during emergency arrivals. A pilot reveals that scans arrive late and patient identities are often ambiguous. Which next action BEST closes the requirements gap before expanding the pilot to additional clinics?

options.text: Ask clinic managers to choose a larger model because their original participation already represents every workflow and exception at reception.
options.why: Manager involvement does not replace observing the specific frontline process that exposed missing requirements during emergency arrivals.

options.text: Add a note telling receptionists to verify every record manually and expand the pilot before defining how late scans are reconciled.
options.why: A warning does not establish a workable identity and timing contract, and expansion would reproduce the unresolved operational gap across more clinics.

options.text: Observe reception reconciliation and map identity, timing, exception ownership, and acceptable degraded behavior with the frontline staff and record owners.
options.why: This establishes the missing workflow constraints and authority boundaries that the extraction benchmark did not capture before wider deployment.

options.text: Increase the extraction benchmark size using the same clean referral letters because higher accuracy will eliminate the emergency reconciliation gap.
options.why: More clean extraction cases do not reproduce late scans or ambiguous patient identity, which are the operational failures discovered in the pilot.

questions.decision: Discovery should examine the real workflow and include people who own its awkward transitions. Observe emergency reconciliation and establish how identity ambiguity and late evidence must be handled. This can change integration and acceptance criteria; additional model benchmarking alone would not reveal the missing operational responsibilities or tolerated failure behavior.

questions.title: Capacity discovery includes the unit
questions.stem: A seed-exchange platform expects 24,000 planting-plan requests in its busiest ten-minute opening period. Each admitted request needs two model calls with no caching benefit assumed. The provisioned allowance is 3,000 model calls per minute. The sponsor proposes promising immediate processing for every arrival. Ignoring other limits, which planning conclusion follows before agreeing to that promise?

options.text: The allowance is sufficient if clients retry throttled calls immediately because retries convert rejected arrivals into additional available processing capacity.
options.why: Retries do not create allowance and can increase contention; immediate processing remains unsupported by the provisioned call budget in the scenario.

options.text: The system needs 48,000 calls per minute because every opening-period request must be counted in the same minute for all planning.
options.why: This treats the ten-minute total as a one-minute average; bursts need separate analysis but do not justify that arithmetic claim.

options.text: The allowance is sufficient because 24,000 requests over ten minutes is only 2,400 calls per minute under the provisioned limit.
options.why: The estimate ignores the two model calls required by each admitted request, so it understates the actual processing demand by half.

options.text: The average demand needs 4,800 calls per minute; obtain capacity or agree bounded queuing before promising immediate processing.
options.why: The calculation includes both calls per user request and the ten-minute interval, revealing a capacity shortfall even before considering bursts.

questions.decision: Demand averages 24,000/10 × 2 = 4,800 calls per minute. The provisioned allowance is short by 1,800 calls per minute, or 18,000 calls over ten minutes. Arrival bursts may worsen the gap. Arrange additional capacity or an explicitly accepted queue and latency envelope before promising immediate service.

questions.title: Give a sponsor a decision
questions.stem: A publisher must choose whether to release an archive assistant to a small paid pilot this month or wait for a broader language pack. The pilot meets its agreed quality gates, but two languages are explicitly unsupported. The board needs a funding decision, while engineers need interface details separately. Which communication BEST supports the board’s choice without hiding the release’s current limits?

options.text: Present the pilot’s successful examples and omit unsupported languages because those languages are already excluded from the engineers’ internal test dataset.
options.why: An internal exclusion does not establish board understanding of the business boundary, and omitting it conceals a material consequence of the release decision.

options.text: Show the architecture’s complete request sequence and ask the board to infer whether the remaining language work merits additional investment.
options.why: The sequence may be accurate but does not explain the cost, timing, and business consequences needed for the board’s funding decision.

options.text: Recommend waiting without describing the viable pilot because presenting two feasible options might weaken confidence in the architect’s preferred course.
options.why: Withholding a feasible alternative prevents the board from evaluating its real trade-off and owning the consequence of the chosen timing.

options.text: Present pilot and delayed-release options with evidence, cost, timing, supported-language limits, and a recommendation tied to explicit expansion criteria.
options.why: The account connects the board’s funding choice to measured outcomes and accepted limitations rather than asking it to infer value from implementation detail.

questions.decision: Present the feasible options with measured value, cost, timing, risk, and the explicit language boundary, then recommend a path with observable expansion conditions. The board needs a decision it can own. Technical detail can support that account but should not replace evidence about the business consequences of the available choices.

questions.title: Record the condition that could reverse it
questions.stem: A materials research team chooses direct API integration for a single deterministic spectrometer service. A partner may later need the same capability through a shared agent environment. The current decision record lists interfaces and today’s cost, but future maintainers cannot tell when to reconsider the choice. Which addition BEST makes the record useful without promising that a different protocol will necessarily be required later?

options.text: Document the rejected alternatives, accepted coupling, and a reassessment trigger if additional clients require shared tool discovery or independently managed integration.
options.why: The record exposes the conditions supporting today’s choice and the changed requirements that could justify reconsideration without predetermining the future outcome.

options.text: Replace the current choice with MCP immediately because any possible future client makes direct integration architecturally invalid today.
options.why: A hypothetical future need does not automatically justify current complexity; the trade-off depends on actual shared requirements and available implementation options.

options.text: State that direct APIs are permanently superior for scientific equipment and prohibit future teams from reopening the integration decision.
options.why: A permanent generalization exceeds the current single-client evidence and prevents adaptation when the explicitly anticipated partner requirements change.

options.text: Add more endpoint diagrams while leaving out alternatives and assumptions because implementation detail lets future maintainers reconstruct the original trade-off.
options.why: Diagrams explain interfaces but cannot reliably recover the unstated decision rationale or identify which changing assumption should trigger a review.

questions.decision: Record the alternatives, why direct integration fits the current constraints, and what evidence would trigger reassessment. A future partner need is a condition to evaluate, not proof that today’s decision is wrong or that MCP is automatically preferable. Useful records explain consequences and the scope of the assumptions behind them.

video_evidence.concept: Record the condition that could reverse it

questions.title: Define the thing users experience
questions.stem: A remote-learning assistant streams an outline quickly but sometimes takes much longer to produce the source-linked lesson plan students actually use. The provider reports time to first token; the school reports time until a usable plan appears. Both measurements are correct. Which TWO agreement changes resolve the mismatch while preserving visibility into both perceived responsiveness and completion of the user’s task?

options.text: Use the school’s completion time but remove required-source validation from the definition so every generated outline can count as a completed plan.
options.why: Removing the required content changes the agreed outcome and makes the metric easier to satisfy without delivering what students actually need.

options.text: Average first-token and completion times into one latency score, allowing faster outlines to compensate for plans that never become usable.
options.why: Combining different events conceals the failure mode and does not establish a defensible service target for either responsiveness or usable completion.

options.text: Retain time to first token as a separate responsiveness indicator and document how degraded or incomplete plans count in the completion measure.
options.why: Keeping the indicators separate preserves useful experience signals while preventing an early partial outline from masquerading as successful task completion.

options.text: Define a user-visible usable-plan completion indicator, including required source links, measurement start, window, population, and percentile calculation.
options.why: This aligns the service target with the actual outcome students need and removes ambiguity about which event stops the completion timer.

options.text: Use the provider’s first-token measurement as the only latency target because streaming means the user has already received the complete service.
options.why: An initial outline does not establish that a usable source-linked lesson plan exists, so the chosen metric would omit the school’s required outcome.

questions.decision: Define distinct responsiveness and usable-completion indicators with shared measurement points, populations, and windows. Specify the output state that counts as usable, including required sources. Neither party’s existing number is inherently wrong; they describe different events, and a service agreement should not use one as a substitute for the other.

questions.title: Tell users where corrections go
questions.stem: A folklore archive assistant accepts curator corrections. The application saves them in a triage queue and includes accepted cases in the next evaluation cycle; it does not change model weights or shared prompts during a conversation. Curators expect each correction to apply globally by the next day. Which response BEST aligns expectations and turns the existing feedback mechanism into an accountable service?

options.text: Stop accepting corrections until the next model release because users’ expectations show that feedback cannot support the current service lifecycle.
options.why: The queue already supports useful evaluation and improvement; the gap is expectation and accountability rather than an absence of a viable feedback mechanism.

options.text: Ask curators to repeat each correction in every session without documenting the queue, so the assistant appears to improve locally over time.
options.why: Repeated local context may affect a session but does not explain or improve the accountable path for validated changes to the shared service.

options.text: Promise that every stored correction changes future model behavior automatically because it is now present somewhere in the application’s feedback database.
options.why: Stored feedback does not alter model weights or shared prompts by itself, and the described application explicitly requires triage and validation before release.

options.text: Publish the correction lifecycle, acknowledgment target, status route, and release cadence, distinguishing saved feedback from validated changes to the shared service.
options.why: This accurately describes the implemented mechanism and gives curators an accountable way to follow corrections without promising automatic global learning.

questions.decision: Explain what is saved, how it is triaged, and when a validated change can reach the shared service. Provide acknowledgment and a status route so feedback is useful to contributors. Saving a correction is not the same as globally learning it, and promising immediate generalization would misrepresent the implemented lifecycle.

questions.title: A handoff contract across three owners
questions.stem: A biodiversity assistant receives field observations through a mobile app, uses a gateway to remove restricted location details, and sends sanitized records to an analysis service. Each component belongs to a different team. The design diagram shows all three boxes but no control ownership, failure contract, or version dependencies. Which THREE additions most directly make the architecture implementable and operable by the receiving teams?

options.text: Add every source-code file to the overview diagram and let receiving engineers infer ownership and safe failure behavior from repository history.
options.why: More internal detail does not establish an explicit cross-team control or failure contract, and inference from history is unreliable during operation.

options.text: Mark the sanitization boundary with its owning team, permitted input and output fields, and evidence that restricted locations do not cross it.
options.why: The owner and field contract establish who enforces the control and what observable behavior the other teams can rely on.

options.text: Record that all teams jointly own sanitization without specifying an execution point, because shared ownership eliminates gaps between component boundaries.
options.why: Undifferentiated shared ownership leaves the actual enforcement step and failure response ambiguous, recreating the handoff gap the document needs to close.

options.text: Specify unavailable and rejected-record responses, retry responsibilities, correlation identifiers, and the escalation route when sanitization cannot complete safely.
options.why: A failure contract prevents teams from inventing incompatible retries or bypasses and makes responsibility for an unsafe intermediate state explicit.

options.text: Version interface schemas and deployment dependencies, linking acceptance checks and rollback guidance to the configuration handed to operations.
options.why: Versioned dependencies and checks help receiving teams deploy compatible components and recover a change without relying on the original architect’s memory.

questions.decision: Document the control at its actual data boundary, the interface behavior on failure, and the versioned operational dependencies. These details turn a component picture into an actionable handoff contract. A meeting or a code reference alone cannot ensure that three teams share the same responsibilities and failure expectations after personnel change.

video_evidence.concept: A handoff contract across three owners

questions.title: Accept the handoff in practice
questions.stem: A coastal archive assistant passes its evaluation gates, and the implementation team prepares to transfer operation to a regional museum. Runbooks exist, but nobody from the museum has exercised restoration, alert acknowledgment, or a configuration rollback. The system will operate during a public exhibition with limited staff. Which next action BEST establishes operational readiness before the museum accepts responsibility?

options.text: Ask the museum to sign that it has read the runbooks, treating written acknowledgment as equivalent evidence to a successful restoration rehearsal.
options.why: Reading establishes awareness but does not test actual permissions, procedures, or infrastructure behavior needed to perform restoration and rollback.

options.text: Transfer responsibility immediately because passed model evaluations establish that infrastructure incidents and configuration rollback will not occur during the exhibition.
options.why: Model quality gates do not validate the receiving team’s operational access or ability to recover infrastructure and configuration failures.

options.text: Keep every alert routed to the original architect until the museum experiences its first incident and learns the system under real pressure.
options.why: The original architect remains a fragile dependency, and learning during a public incident does not establish readiness before the responsibility transfer.

options.text: Run a joint operational rehearsal covering alert response, access, restoration, and rollback, then close identified gaps before formal acceptance.
options.why: The receiving team demonstrates the actual responsibilities it will own, testing both the documentation and the configured operational paths before the exhibition.

questions.decision: Exercise the operating responsibilities with the team that will own them and use the results as handoff evidence. Written runbooks are necessary but do not establish that access, alerts, restoration, and rollback work in practice. The rehearsal can expose gaps while the implementation team is available to fix them.

questions.title: Expand on observed operating evidence
questions.stem: A citizen-history assistant has completed a proof of concept on curated records. A limited live pilot then reveals unusual document formats and external catalogue timeouts, both recoverable through existing human routes. The sponsor wants nationwide release immediately. Which deployment proposal BEST balances expanding value with learning from the unrepresented operating conditions rather than repeating the same curated demonstration?

options.text: Delay every expansion until the external catalogue can guarantee zero future timeouts, regardless of the demonstrated recovery path and accepted service goals.
options.why: An absolute external guarantee is not the stated acceptance requirement; controlled expansion can evaluate bounded recovery instead of demanding impossible certainty.

options.text: Release nationwide because recoverable pilot failures prove that human routes will scale automatically to every region’s document and catalogue conditions.
options.why: The existence of a recovery route does not establish its nationwide capacity or effectiveness across the newly expanded operating population.

options.text: Expand in bounded waves after validating format handling, timeout recovery, owner response, and rollback against pilot-derived acceptance criteria.
options.why: The staged plan targets the actual operating uncertainty and allows broader value when measured evidence supports the next population increase.

options.text: Repeat the curated proof of concept until its score improves, then treat the higher score as evidence that live catalogue timeouts are resolved.
options.why: The curated dataset does not exercise the new operational failure classes, so a higher score would not answer the rollout-readiness question.

questions.decision: Use staged expansion with observable gates tied to the failure classes discovered in live operation. Exercise recovery and rollback, then widen the population when the evidence supports it. A successful curated proof of concept does not measure nationwide operational diversity, while repeating it unchanged would not address the new uncertainty.

questions.title: Policy inheritance is not a local exception
questions.stem: A research institute centrally denies a particular Claude Code tool. A project team adds an allow rule for a narrower use of that tool and assumes the narrower rule wins. The institute intends the central denial to remain binding until administrators review it. Which configuration response BEST respects the documented permission precedence while giving the project a concrete route to resolve its legitimate workflow need?

options.text: Move the allow rule into the project’s instruction file because instructions are evaluated after managed settings and therefore take precedence.
options.why: Instruction text does not change the enforced permission policy, and moving the request there cannot legitimately override the central denial.

options.text: Verify the effective managed denial, keep it enforced, and ask its owner to review a narrowly scoped replacement or centrally approved policy change.
options.why: The approach respects deny precedence while making the workflow need concrete for the authority that can legitimately alter the managed boundary.

options.text: Disable all managed settings for this repository because a project with a valid research purpose can define its own independent tool policy.
options.why: The project’s legitimate need does not authorize removing institute controls; the intended exception process belongs to the managed-policy owner.

options.text: Keep the project allow rule because a narrower argument pattern always overrides a broader managed denial for the same tool.
options.why: Documented deny precedence is not replaced by specificity, so a local allow does not carve an exception out of the binding denial.

questions.decision: Claude Code evaluates deny rules before ask and allow rules, and managed controls cannot be bypassed through a narrower local allow. Verify the effective policy and take the requested exception to its owner. If appropriate, administrators can change the governed boundary or provide a separately authorized narrower capability after review.

video_evidence.concept: Policy inheritance is not a local exception

questions.title: Independent checks for a generated change
questions.stem: A team asks Claude Code to modify a sediment-analysis parser. The existing implementation treats missing readings as zero, but the agreed requirement says they remain missing. Generated tests copied the existing zero behavior and pass. Which TWO workflow changes best establish the intended semantics and provide an independent check, rather than simply raising coverage around the same mistaken assumption?

options.text: Generate more tests from the current parser’s outputs because a larger passing suite demonstrates that the revised implementation preserves intended semantics.
options.why: A larger suite can reinforce the same incorrect oracle and does not establish the requirement that missing readings remain distinct from zero.

options.text: Compare code coverage before and after the change and approve if coverage rises, without checking whether fixture expectations match the agreed requirement.
options.why: Coverage shows execution, not correctness of the expected behavior, and cannot resolve whether the tests encode missing values or incorrect zeroes.

options.text: Review the diff in fresh context against the missing-value contract and run downstream calculations that distinguish missing readings from measured zeroes.
options.why: Independent review and integration checks test the semantic consequence that a generated unit suite mirroring the old behavior failed to expose.

options.text: Create requirement-derived missing-value fixtures and confirm they fail against the old behavior before accepting the parser implementation change.
options.why: The failing fixtures establish an independent behavioral oracle for missing readings rather than copying the current implementation’s incorrect zero substitution.

options.text: Let the authoring session rewrite every failing expected value until the entire suite passes, treating consistency with code as the source of truth.
options.why: Rewriting expectations to match implementation removes the independent behavioral check and can preserve the exact missing-value defect the team must correct.

questions.decision: Establish expected behavior from the requirement before accepting generated tests, then review the change with independent context and run the relevant integration checks. Test-first work is useful when its oracle is independently grounded. More assertions or self-review cannot compensate for tests that encode the wrong missing-value contract.

video_evidence.concept: Independent checks for a generated change

questions.title: Find the event before proposing the fix
questions.stem: A photogrammetry build fails intermittently after a worker is rescheduled. The available logs span many gigabytes and contain occasional credentials in unrelated lines. Claude Code can search local files under a restricted account. Which debugging approach BEST preserves the evidence needed to distinguish a race from an environment mismatch while reducing unnecessary context and secret exposure?

options.text: Search by failed job and time window, redact secrets, compare successful and failed schedules, then reproduce the leading hypothesis with a focused check.
options.why: The approach preserves causal evidence while limiting context and exposure, and it produces a testable explanation before changing the intermittent build behavior.

options.text: Add two retries to the build and close the incident once the next rescheduled worker succeeds, using that success as proof of root cause.
options.why: A successful retry shows the symptom is intermittent but does not distinguish a race from an environment mismatch or establish that either was fixed.

options.text: Delete failed-run logs after recording the error message so the next reproduction starts with a cleaner context and less confusing historical evidence.
options.why: The surrounding schedule and environment events may be necessary to explain the failure; deleting them removes evidence rather than narrowing it safely.

options.text: Upload every log unchanged and ask for a complete repair because broader context guarantees the agent can distinguish race conditions from environment mismatches.
options.why: Unfiltered volume does not guarantee useful reasoning and unnecessarily exposes credentials without first narrowing the causal evidence relevant to the failing job.

questions.decision: Start with bounded, redacted evidence around the failed job and compare it with a successful counterpart. Build a reproducible hypothesis from correlated events before proposing a repair. Tool-assisted narrowing is useful because large raw logs contain irrelevant and sensitive material; retries alone can conceal the cause without explaining it.

video_evidence.concept: Find the event before proposing the fix

questions.title: Contain a credential exposure
questions.stem: While investigating an indexing outage, an engineer pastes a configuration file containing a live service token into an assistant session. The token can read restricted source documents and is still active. The incident owner has authority to rotate it and preserve necessary audit evidence. Which response BEST addresses the existing exposure and improves the next investigation without pretending that deleting a message recalls every copy?

options.text: Rotate the token, review relevant access under the incident procedure, and use redacted configuration plus restricted tooling for subsequent diagnosis.
options.why: Rotation contains future credential use, while the audit and safer diagnostic path address the exposure and reduce recurrence without destroying necessary evidence.

options.text: Delete the message and continue using the token because removing its visible text revokes access from every system that may have processed it.
options.why: Message deletion does not revoke a credential or prove removal of all copies, so its live authority remains a material unresolved exposure.

options.text: Encode the same token in base64 before sharing the file again because encoding prevents both the assistant and downstream readers from recovering it.
options.why: Base64 is reversible encoding rather than secret protection, and sharing the encoded live token preserves the same underlying credential-exposure risk.

options.text: Ask the assistant to forget the token and replace the configuration filename, preserving the credential to avoid disrupting the ongoing indexing investigation.
options.why: A model instruction does not invalidate the credential or establish that other retained copies cannot be used while the investigation continues.

questions.decision: Invalidate the exposed credential, investigate its use under the incident procedure, and repair the evidence-sharing path with redaction and access boundaries. Rotation changes the credential’s future authority; deleting visible text does not prove all copies disappeared. Preserve audit evidence according to the incident owner’s scope rather than destroying it as a cleanup shortcut.

drills.title: Evidence-boundary checks
drills.stem: Judge whether each proposal satisfies its specific stated obligation. Answer Yes or No independently; these unscored checks do not imply a fixed number of Yes answers.

rows.text: A catalogue search requires current rights status. The serving indexes exclude withdrawn records, while a separately authorized archive remains inaccessible to answers.
rows.why: Serving eligibility is enforced without confusing that boundary with a separate archival obligation.

rows.text: A table extraction loses column labels. Adding overlap to the same flattened numeric text establishes which cultivar each confidence interval belongs to.
rows.why: Overlap does not reconstruct associations already lost during extraction.

rows.text: A model judge passes all known-good examples. This alone establishes that it detects fluent explanations with reversed scientific causality.
rows.why: The negative semantic failure has never been tested.

rows.text: A worker returns two completed zones and explicit missing-zone status. The orchestrator preserves those gaps after its bounded retry expires.
rows.why: The report accurately distinguishes usable observations from uncompleted coverage.

rows.text: A model-specific input estimate includes embedded images and local tool schemas. The admission service also reserves a conservative margin.
rows.why: The full supported request is counted, and the estimate is not treated as an exact guarantee.

drills.title: Operational-accountability checks
drills.stem: Decide whether each conclusion follows from the stated evidence. Judge each independently; these are unscored companion exercises.

rows.text: A cached prefix contains a unique identifier before its breakpoint. Extending its TTL makes different identifiers match the same prefix.
rows.why: Expiration and prefix equality are different properties.

rows.text: A queue carries trace context and workers extract it into their spans. This supports causal request tracing across asynchronous processing.
rows.why: Explicit context propagation connects the stages instead of relying on timestamp proximity.

rows.text: A service values freed staff hours as usable capacity. Calling that figure a payroll saving requires additional evidence about actual expenditure.
rows.why: Capacity value and reduced cash spending are different business outcomes.

rows.text: Counsel confirms a ninety-day retention scope across identifiable exports and indexes. Expiring only the source object implements that full scope.
rows.why: The other covered copies still require the stipulated lifecycle action.

rows.text: A read-only tool is deferred from initial context but discoverable later. Deferral alone revokes any write authority in its credential.
rows.why: Discovery controls context loading; credential authorization remains a separate boundary.

drills.title: Match the immediate engineering task
drills.stem: Choose the BEST immediate task for each observed gap. Choices may repeat, and these five rows are unscored.

rows.text: Cultivar yield values have lost their column headers during PDF ingestion.
rows.why: The source associations need correction before a generation model can reliably use them.

rows.text: A streaming provider times the first token, while students time a complete source-linked lesson plan.
rows.why: The parties measure different completion events and need an agreed outcome definition.

rows.text: The model judge has seen correct subtitles but no fluent subtitles that reverse the actor.
rows.why: The untested negative class must challenge the judge’s ability to discriminate semantic failures.

rows.text: The receiving museum has runbooks but has never restored a backup or acknowledged its own alert.
rows.why: A practical exercise tests whether the receiving team can execute its responsibilities.

rows.text: The index finds the correct research trial, but row values are detached from cultivar identity and units.
rows.why: The repeated category is intentional: lost evidence structure is still the immediate failure.
